SAL induces cellular senescence in various PCa models mediated by the AR, activation of AKT signaling and hypophosphorylation of pRb. Here, we show that SAL upregulates the lncRNA CD44-DT, the CD44 divergent transcript, in PCa cells linking CD44-DT to AR signaling. Knockdown and overexpression datasets suggest that CD44-DT supresses SAL-induced senescence as a negative feed-back loop. Transcriptome, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq analyses of PCa cells reveal that AR is recruited to the first intron of CD44 gene locus. Transcriptome analyses of the knockdown suggests that members of AP-1 family act in concert with AR as an upstream activator of CD44-DT. Accordingly, inhibition of the AP-1 complex by a small molecule inhibitor results in downregulation of CD44-DT expression, enhanced SAL-induced senescence and reduced proliferation. Mechanistically, CD44-DT physically interacts with PCNA and AR. This interaction facilitates p21 tumor suppressor degradation, permits cyclin-CDK activation, retinoblastoma (Rb) hyperphosphorylation activation of the AKT-p70S6K pathway. These findings suggest that CD44-DT is part of AR signaling and acts as a novel onco-lncRNA that is upregulated by AR. To validate the role of AR, we engineered a chimeric ncRNA capable degrading the AR as a novel type of RNA-PROTAC. Accordingly, this RNA-based AR-degrader downregulates CD44-DT confirming AR regulation of CD44-DT. Interestingly, the RNA-PROTAC potently induces apoptosis. Thus, the data suggest that CD44-DT is a novel direct AR target gene that modulates PCNA and p21 protein stability identifying a novel negative feed-back loop at the crossroad between proliferation and senescence indicating CD44-DT as a potential therapeutic target for PCa.

items.title: Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) interacts with BRG1 chromatin remodeler and regulates neuronal activity-induced gene activation
items.corresponding_institution: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
items.abstract: SWI/SNF-like BAF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes play important roles in neural development and plasticity by regulating neural gene expression, especially in response to neuronal stimulations. Previously, we have shown that BRG1, the core subunit of BAF, undergoes neuronal activity-induced phosphorylation, which is important for the expression of a group of activity regulated genes (ARGs). Proteomic analyses identified Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) as a novel BRG1 interacting protein. Neuronal depolarization induces nuclear enrichment of DCLK1 and increases interactions between BRG1 and DCLK1. We showed that the DCLK1 kinase domain and BRG1 C-terminal fragments are sufficient to mediate their interaction. Thus, DCLK1 is a candidate kinase responsible for BRG1 phosphorylation in response to neuronal activation. Using DCLK1 specific inhibitors and kinase inactive mutations, we showed that DCLK1, in a kinase activity dependent manner, promotes BRG1 phosphorylation and ARG activation. Thus, we identified a novel interacting kinase of BAF chromatin remodeling complex that regulates ARG expression. Because abnormal expression and mutations of both BAF complexes and DCLK1 are associated with neural disorders and cancer, our study provides molecular insights into their functions in these diseases.

items.title: An open-source semi-automated workflow for multi-omics sample extraction
items.abstract: Multiomics analysis relies on extracting metabolites lipids and proteins from a single sample A widely used method for this is Metabolomics Proteomics and Lipidomics Extraction MPLEx a triphasic chloroform methanol water extraction but it is manually intensive and depends on skilled operators working around a fragile protein layer Here we present OpenMPLEx a semi automated MPLEx workflow for low cost open source Opentrons liquid handlers A minor change in chemistry pellets the protein so that a robot can collect the aqueous and organic phases from above We compared the automated workflow with two manual MPLEx protocols by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry LC MS based proteomics lipidomics and metabolomics The methods were roughly equivalent and measured similar differences between growth media We then scaled the workflow to 96 well plates and tested it on an 80 sample Pseudomonas putida experiment One operator took all 80 samples from cell pellets to LC MS data in a working week with about 3 h of hands on time rather than days at the bench and quantified about 3 900 protein groups All scripts labware definitions and print files are open source so that other laboratories can adapt the workflow

items.title: Convergent Genomic Signatures of Selection in Thar: Genetic trade-offs for desert survival
items.abstract: Background: Desert environments provide a setting for natural biological experiments to cope up with simultaneous stressors of extreme temperatures, aridity, UV exposure, and limited food resources. Biological adaptations that support living in such an environment could become liabilities when the environment and lifestyle change due to gene-environment mismatch. We explored whether genetically and culturally diverse endogamous native populations of the Thar exhibit convergent signatures of selection to desert conditions and whether the selected loci have implications in traits and disease susceptibilities relevant to non-native transitions. Results: We report 348 high-confidence variants across 45 candidate genes from a study on 176 individuals from eight genetically distinct Thar populations. These genes identified from humans and other desert inhabitants display convergent evolution with multiple selection scans (PBSn1, Tajima`s D, iHS, and XPEHH) in diverse Thar populations. Prominent genes include ZNF385D, SGCZ, SARDH, SLC12A3, etc. Selected variants essential in the desert environment were associated with complex traits like lipid metabolism, hypertension, renal and cardiovascular diseases, and addiction in GWAS and PheWAS. Noteworthy, in a syntenic locus, eQTLs in SARDH, which modulates DBH implicated in addiction, suggest a potential link with survival advantage in an uncertain desert environment. Likewise, a selected variant (rs7204044) in SLC12A3, implicated in hypertension in non-desert populations, seems to be a key to water-salt homeostasis in desert natives. Conclusions: These findings suggest that variants linked to adaptive traits in desert conditions could be linked to maladaptation in an altered environment. This has potential health consequences in climatic and lifestyle transitions among native inhabitants.

items.title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
items.corresponding_institution: Genomics and Regulatory Systems Unit, Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University
items.abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

items.title: ATR coordinates nuclear and cytoskeletal mechanics during leukemic migration
items.corresponding_institution: Centro de Investigaciones Biologicas Margarita Salas, CIB Margarita Salas-CSIC
items.abstract: Mechanical adaptation is essential for tumor cells to cross physical barriers during dissemination, but the mechanisms linking genome-stress signalling to cellular mechanics remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that ATR (ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related kinase) acts as a dual regulator of nuclear and cytoskeletal adaptations in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of ATR altered nuclear architecture and mechanical behaviour, increasing nuclear deformability in 3D confined conditions. Mechanistically, ATR inhibition increased chromatin accessibility, H3K4me3 levels and the association of WDR5 with chromatin. In parallel, ATR interference reduced myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) expression, ERM phosphorylation and the association between ERM proteins and actin, consistent with altered cortical cytoskeletal regulation. These changes had distinct consequences in leukemic cell migration: ATR inhibition promoted T-ALL migration through confined 3D environments but impaired transendothelial migration and reduced early homing to peripheral tissues in vivo. Inhibition of Chk-1 did not reproduce the nuclear response to ATR inhibition, suggesting that these effects might not depend on the ATR-Chk-1 axis signalling. Together, our findings identify ATR as a regulator of nuclear and cortical organization during leukemic migration, revealing that enhanced nuclear deformability might be insufficient to promote migration across diverse physical microenvironments.

items.title: NXP800 suppresses HSF1 through coordinated stress signaling and GCN2-dependent translational repression in glioblastoma
items.abstract: Under states of proteotoxic stress, Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1) serves as the primary transcription factor responsible for restoring protein homeostasis. General Control Nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) similarly alleviates cellular stress. Activated by a shortage in amino acids, GCN2 triggers the phosphorylation of eIF2 to downregulate global protein synthesis while selectively translating survival-promoting proteins like Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4). Cancer cells often exploit these pathways to mitigate damage from rapid proliferation and metabolic demands. In Glioblastoma (GBM), HSF1 promotes tumor growth and apoptosis evasion, while GCN2 maintains cancer cell homeostasis and survival. NXP800 has recently emerged as both an HSF1 inhibitor and GCN2 agonist with potent antitumor activity, yet the mechanism by which these pathways integrate to modulate GBM fate remains unclear. Herein, we show NXP800 induces an initial, GCN2-independent downregulation of HSF1 transcriptional activity, followed by a delayed, GCN2-p-eIF2-dependent decrease in HSF1 translation. This temporal regulation is accompanied by altered phosphorylation of the HSF1-activating kinase AKT1. Furthermore, we show NXP800 directly engages the HSF1 protein and that HSF1 suppression is important for the NXP800 anti-proliferative effects. Analysis of cell line and patient data further establishes a negative correlation between GCN2 and HSF1 signaling across multiple cancer types, including GBM. Collectively, our data provide a molecular framework for the dual inhibitory action of NXP800 and offers a comprehensive understanding of how this compound impairs cancer progression.

items.title: Targeting AURKA by CRISPR/SaCas9 Alters Cell Cycle Progression and Enhances Lenvatinib-Associated Reduction in Cell Viability in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: An Integrated In Silico and HepG2 in Vitro Study
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presents substantial clinical concerns as a result of its high treatment resistance, frequent recurrence, and strong correlation with chronic liver diseases. Aurora kinase A (AURKA) is overexpressed in HCC correlating with poor prognosis and treatment resistance. Our bioinformatics analyses revealed that AURKA overexpression in HCC is associated with mitotic proteins and oncogenes, emphasizing its role in cancer progression. CRISPR/SaCas9-mediated AURKA knockdown markedly reduced AURKA expression levels through inducing several indels in the AURKA gene sequence, resulting in functional consequences including upregulation of p21, p53, and caspase-8, as well as downregulation of CDK1, CDK2, PI3K (alpha subunit), P38, and BCL-2 genes. Flow cytometry verified that these alterations were compatible with G2-phase cell cycle arrest and slight activation of apoptosis. Also, scratch and colony formation assays indicated a significant reduction in metastatic and proliferative potential. Furthermore, AURKA knockdown combined with Lenvatinib significantly reduce HepG2 cell viability compared with either treatment alone. Mechanistically, this study indicated that AURKA suppression reduced cell viability/proliferation by the modulation of oncogenic PI3K/AKT and p38/MAPK pathways. These in-silico and in-vitro findings highlight the critical role of AURKA in HCC pathogenesis. Here, the CRISPR/SaCas9-mediated genetic disruption of AURKA reveals its mechanistic role in regulating cell cycle, apoptosis, and tumor-suppressor signalling. Our study demonstrates AURKA as a potential molecular target to suppress HCC, while providing genetic evidence that its downregulation enhances Lenvatinib effect.

items.title: Quantification of cannabidiolic acid in Cannabis sativa using a two-component allosteric protein biosensor
items.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.

items.title: A modular workflow for biomedical entity normalization across heterogeneous biological ontologies
items.abstract: Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying rare diseases requires integrating information about phenotypes, cell types, anatomical structures, and molecular functions and processes. Although some of this knowledge is available in structured resources, additional relationships remain dispersed across biomedical literature. Extracting and integrating this information requires normalizing heterogeneous biological entities against specialized ontologies. This motivated the development of a common biomedical named entity normalization (NEN) workflow and the evaluation of its performance across different entity types and ontologies. We developed a modular NEN workflow combining exact matching, lexical and semantic candidate retrieval, and reranking, without requiring ontology-specific training. Candidate retrieval integrates BM25, fuzzy matching, character n-gram similarity, and SapBERT. We evaluated the workflow across the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), Cell Ontology (CL), Uberon, and Gene Ontology (GO) using multiple benchmarks, separately assessing candidate retrieval, reranking accuracy, and overall normalization accuracy. We also investigated factors associated with retrieval difficulty and compared the workflow with CellExLink, a specialized cell-type normalization system. Retrieval performance varied across ontologies and benchmarks, with lexical and semantic methods providing complementary candidate coverage in some settings. Increasing candidate-set size improved retrieval recall but did not necessarily improve overall normalization accuracy, as larger candidate sets could reduce reranking performance. Retrieval difficulty was associated with mention characteristics and ontology categories. Our evaluation identifies the performance characteristics and limitations of a common normalization workflow across heterogeneous biological ontologies, highlighting the importance of assessing candidate retrieval and selection separately. The workflow provides a methodological foundation for extracting and integrating biological information from rare disease literature, with potential applicability to other biomedical information-extraction tasks requiring normalization against these ontologies.

items.title: Visual Search and ASD: Basic vs. Superordinate Category Search
items.abstract: We study visual search and categorization among individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and a neuro-typical comparison group (NT). Individuals with ASD often exhibit distinct sensory processing patterns and may face challenges in efficiently detecting and categorizing visual stimuli. They may also process categories differently compared to NT groups, reflecting variations in typical sensory processing mechanisms. Based on our previous findings, this study employs visual search categorization tasks, testing reaction time and set-size slopes for different target categories. Participants included 26 individuals with ASD and 11 NT individuals, with similar mean ages and mean IQ Block Design subtest scores. They performed basic-level and superordinate-level visual search, as well as a categorization task. In the visual search task, participants identified targets within arrays of varying set sizes (4, 16, 36, 64). Face detection remained rapid across groups, and Basic-level search was similar in ASD and NT groups (mean set-size slopes: 48.7 and 45 ms/item, respectively). In contrast, superordinate search was much slower in ASD (99 ms/item) compared to NT (70.8 ms/item), reflecting increased cognitive demands. Object typicality influenced performance, with less typical items being slower to both categorize and detect. These findings suggest that basic-level processing is relatively preserved in ASD, whereas superordinate categorization imposes greater demands. The results highlight the role of typicality and support differences in perceptual and cognitive processing in ASD. Our findings contribute to better understanding visual cognition in autism and may inform strategies for improving conceptual generalization and visual learning.

items.title: Unified CEBRA learns shared neural latents across recordings to map single-neuron contributions to population codes
items.abstract: Neural computation is thought to rely on distributed populations; however, most single recording samples capture only a fraction of them, and rare cell types may contribute only a small proportion of neurons per session. Pooling many recordings could reveal how these populations encode information, but each recording samples different neurons, so their contributions cannot be easily compared directly. Here we show that recordings can be combined into a single model of all recorded neurons by aligning them with a shared label, used at both training and inference, placing every neuron's contribution to the population code on a common scale. This approach, called Unified CEBRA, retained interpretable task information across recordings in the monkey and mouse sensorimotor cortex, rat hippocampus, and mouse visual cortex. Pooling thousands of excitatory and inhibitory neurons from hundreds of sessions from mouse visual cortex, we found that the neurons that contributed most to the model's readout of visual features were not only the most strongly tuned, but also those that responded more reliably and were less coupled to co-recorded neurons. Unified CEBRA, therefore, can unveil coding principles studied at the population scale with mappable features to individual neurons from sparse, multi-session recordings using our new approach.

items.title: Dissociable patterns of neurophysiological alterations during guided search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
items.corresponding_institution: Nathan S. Kline Institute for Psychiatric Research, Orangeburg, NY, United States
items.abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p[≤].038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Overall, the findings support bottom-up disturbances of visual processing in schizophrenia. In autism, pre-onset alpha was higher and task-related suppression was larger.

items.title: Keratinocyte IL-17RA signaling promotes neutrophil recruitment and clinical lesions in experimental epidermolysis bullosa
items.corresponding_institution: lnfection Immunology, Research Centre Borstel, Germany
items.abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is an autoimmune blistering disease (AIBD) characterized by anti-type VII collagen autoantibody-mediated tissue injury. Neutrophils have been identified as essential for dermal-epidermal separation in various in vitro and mouse models of EBA. Although interleukin-17 (IL-17) signaling promotes neutrophilic inflammation, its contribution to EBA and the relevant responding cell types remain poorly defined. We investigated the role and cellular targets of IL-17 receptor A (IL-17RA) signaling using an antibody-transfer model of EBA in mice with global IL-17RA deficiency, combined IL-17A/IL-17F deficiency, IL-17F deficiency, or myeloid cell- or keratinocyte-specific IL-17RA deletion. Complementary in vitro assays assessed IL-17A-induced chemokine expression and neutrophil migration. Global IL-17RA deficiency, combined IL-17A/IL-17F deficiency, and IL-17F deficiency significantly reduced disease severity in vivo. Keratinocyte-specific IL-17RA deletion markedly attenuated EBA, whereas myeloid cell-specific deletion did not confer protection. In vitro, IL-17A increased Cxcl1 mRNA expression in keratinocytes and fibroblasts, and conditioned media from stimulated cells promoted neutrophil migration. These findings identify keratinocytes as key cellular targets of IL-17RA signaling in experimental EBA and support a mechanism linking epithelial cytokine responses to neutrophil recruitment and tissue injury. Our data support investigating the keratinocyte IL-17RA pathway as a potential therapeutic target in EBA and related AIBD.

items.title: TRAIT: A Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates for CRISPR/Cas- and Integrase-Mediated Genome Engineering
items.abstract: The generation of genetically engineered mammalian cell models often requires repeated construction of integration donors that differ in their targeting sequences, genetic payloads, or integration strategies. Although modular DNA assembly methods facilitate construct generation, adapting existing expression cassettes to different genome-engineering applications remains labor-intensive. Here, we present TRAIT (Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates), a modular cloning framework that combines direct Golden Gate assembly of targeting elements with Gateway-mediated transfer of genetic payloads. The core vector architecture separates genome-targeting sequences from payload assembly, allowing existing Gateway-compatible constructs to be reused without modification of internal Type IIS restriction sites. We developed vector modules supporting homology-directed repair, homology-independent targeted integration, FrameSelect-compatible donor cleavage, coordinated guide RNA delivery, inducible Cas9 expression, Bxb1-mediated cassette exchange, and conditional transgene expression. An extended MultiSite Gateway workflow enables the assembly of complex integration donors using independently prepared regulatory modules, including components from the Mammalian ToolKit. Functional validation in human cells demonstrated targeted integration, recombinase-mediated cassette exchange, and multiplexed genome editing. We further applied TRAIT to generate human induced pluripotent stem cells carrying functional doxycycline-inducible Cas9 and candidate landing-pad integration constructs. Together, these results establish TRAIT as an interoperable framework for assembling and deploying diverse genome-engineering constructs in mammalian cells.

items.title: An atlas of the sRNAs and their targets in Staphylococcus aureus
items.corresponding_institution: Genetics and Experimental Bioinformatics, Faculty of Biology, Institute of Biology III, University of Freiburg, Germany
items.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is an opportunistic pathogen that causes various diseases in animals and humans. Small RNAs (sRNAs) control major steps in the infection process and acclimation responses, contributing to the architecture of the regulatory networks. However, a large number of putative sRNAs remain poorly characterized. Here we present aureoRNA, an interactive database (https://aurorna.biologie.uni-freiburg.de) that integrates available information for each sRNA, including phylogeny in the phylum Bacillota, public transcriptome datasets for sRNA and mRNA correlation, and permits computational predictions of sRNA functions. The aureoRNA-based analysis of the sRNA RsaD revealed new targets including the oxidative threonine catabolism and the arginine deiminase pathway. A target-centric search identifying potential sRNAs for mRNAs of interest revealed the citZ citrate synthase mRNA as an RsaE target, and two small prophage genes as RNAIII interaction partner. The aureoRNA database facilitates the functional characterization of the entire set of sRNAs and their targets in this major pathogen.

items.title: Modelling Maternal-to-Zygotic Transition Dynamics to Identify Common Gene Expression Baselines in Zebrafish Development.
items.abstract: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.

items.title: Tracking the trajectory of individual conjugative plasmids in bacterial communities using CRISPR acquisition-based recording
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto de Biomedicina y Biotecnologia de Cantabria - Universidad de Cantabria
items.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer mediated by conjugative plasmids is a primary driver of bacterial evolution and the spread of adaptive traits, including antibiotic resistance determinants. Tracking how these plasmids disseminate through complex microbial communities remains a major challenge. Current methodologies often yield static, endpoint snapshots of host identity, overlooking transient transfer events and plasmid encounters with the co-resident mobilome. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SPacer Integration (SPI) plasmids, which turn the mobile element itself into a recorder of its own transfer history. We engineered conjugative and mobilizable plasmids to carry a CRISPR-Cas adaptation cassette (cas1-cas2 and a minimal CRISPR array) and maintain tight repression of cas1-cas2 expression in the donor cell, so that upon transfer they capture spacers from the chromosome and plasmids of new hosts and store them permanently in their own array. Subsequent PCR amplification and sequencing of these expanded arrays provide a molecular record of both the bacterial hosts and the co-resident plasmids encountered. We created SPI plasmids using the backbones of well-characterized mobilizable and conjugative plasmids RSF1010, RP4, F, and R100-1. We tested SPI plasmids in defined laboratory matings and in complex wastewater communities. The analysis of the acquired spacers successfully mapped permissive host ranges and profiled the co-resident plasmids in situ. Requiring only standard cloning, PCR and sequencing, this accessible and cost-effective strategy establishes a new framework for studying plasmid ecology. Because spacers are integrated chronologically, it further offers the potential to reconstruct multi-step transfer trajectories across natural microbial networks.

items.title: New medium for the production of Dermacentor reticulatus and Ixodes persulcatus tick primary cell lines
items.corresponding_institution: FBRI State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology Vector Rospotrebnadzor
items.abstract: Background. The increasing prevalence of diseases caused by vector borne infections is an important public health problem. Currently, over 1000 extant tick species have been identified worldwide, and approximately ten percent of them are known to be vectors of pathogens (protozoa, bacteria, and viruses), leading to diseases in animals and humans. Tick cell lines are increasingly being used in research on tick physiology and the pathogens of vector borne infections. To obtain and maintain tick cell lines, traditionally used L-15-based nutrient media. However, obtaining a continuous tick cell line remains a complex and time consuming process. Therefore, it is important to develop new methods that can accelerate the process of obtaining tick cell cultures. Methods. To establish primary tick cell lines, we used, for the first time, a ready-made DMEM/F12 + GlutaMAX culture medium supplemented with 20% fetal bovine serum. Results. In this study, it was shown that DMEM/F12 + GlutaMAX nutrient medium is suitable for obtaining primary cell cultures of two species of ticks from two different genera of the family Ixodidae. Primary cell lines of the tick Ixodes persulcatus were obtained for the first time. We also managed to accelerate the process of obtaining subcultures: the first subcultures were obtained within 1-2 months of tick tissue isolation. Conclusions. This new method, allows us to overcome several existing technical difficulties. It is likely that the DMEM/F12 + Glutamax medium can also be used to obtain and maintain tick cell lines of other species. Thus, an alternative to the traditionally used L-15-based media has emerged, allowing researchers to select the medium most suitable for their tasks. The rapid production of subcultures creates opportunities to conduct certain studies directly on primary cultures, without waiting for their transformation into an immortal culture.

items.title: Activity-based fluorescence screening uncovers host enzymatic responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection
items.corresponding_institution: Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo
items.abstract: Transcriptomic and proteomic studies have characterized host responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection, yet changes in endogenous enzymatic activities remain poorly understood. Here, we screened 89 enzyme-activatable fluorescence probes in living SARS-CoV-2-infected Calu-3 cells and identified 18 probes showing enhanced fluorescence, with some exhibiting multiplicity-of-infection-dependent responses. Neither SARS-CoV-2 Mpro nor PLpro activated the tested probes, and several did not exhibit comparable fluorescence enhancements in influenza-virus-infected cells. Target identification and biochemical validation implicated calpain-1 (CAPN1) and puromycin-sensitive aminopeptidase (PSA) as major contributors to probe activation. A PSA-reactive fluorescence probe confirmed that SARS-CoV-2-infected living cells showed enhanced PSA activity, which was suppressed by puromycin. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed a strong positive correlation between PSA and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein signals. Notably, neither CAPN1 nor PSA was included among differentially expressed genes or proteins previously identified in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells. These findings highlight activity-based fluorescence screening as a complementary strategy to expression-based analyses for discovering infection-induced biomarker enzymes.

items.title: Breastfeeding Enables Systemic Transfer of Functional Maternal Immune Cells to Neonates
items.abstract: Does breastfeeding transfer living maternal immune cells that persist and function in offspring, beyond providing soluble immune factors? Using a foster-nursing mouse model that eliminates prenatal exposure, this study directly tests whether maternal cells can be transferred postnatally through breastmilk. We found that intact maternal immune cells survive neonatal gastrointestinal transit, enter the circulation, and disseminate to peripheral organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing shows that transferred cells span multiple hematopoietic lineages, dominated by monocyte-derived macrophages with a distinct stress-adapted, inflammatory transcriptional state compatible with persistence in the neonatal environment. Interestingly, these maternal cells are detected at sites of neonatal tissue injury, consistent with chemotactic responsiveness. Our findings suggest that breastfeeding may serve as a postnatal route for maternal cellular transfer, potentially extending maternal immune influence beyond gestation.

items.title: Disentangling genomic imprinting from indirect parental genetic effects on the human methylome
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Science and Technology Austria
items.abstract: Imprinted genes regulate development and metabolism and are implicated in both rare developmental syndromes and common diseases. Genomic imprinting is conventionally inferred from parent-of-origin effects (POEs), identified as differences between heterozygotes who inherited an allele from their mother and those who inherited it from their father. However, such differences can also be caused by indirect parental genetic effects, i.e. the fact that the genotype of a parent can be associated with behavioral or environmental changes that affect the phenotype of their offspring. No study of the human methylome has so far accounted for this confounding effect when inferring imprinted loci. Here, we jointly estimate direct, maternal, paternal and parent-of-origin effects at 850,055 methylation probes from whole blood in 2,438 parent-offspring trios from Generation Scotland. Of 5,435 probes with apparent POE signal, 4,974 (91.5%) fall below threshold once parental genotypes are included, suggesting that the vast majority are not attributable to imprinting alone. We treat the 281 remaining probes, 17 on the X chromosome and 42 not previously reported, as a conservative, high-confidence set, map them to 1,118 SNP loci linked to gene expression and protein abundance, and identify 27 probes where imprinting and indirect parental genetic effects both contribute. In a hold-out set of relatives, 250 of the 281 show familial resemblance consistent with a combination of imprinting and parental effects. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for indirect parental genetic effects when interpreting putative imprinting regions.

items.title: Generation of a Public Dataset for Etiological Subtyping with the Genomic Cluster Engine
items.corresponding_institution: NVIDIA, Inc., 95051, Santa Clara, CA, United States
items.abstract: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.

items.title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
items.abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

items.title: The KMT2A-MENIN complex is a therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia
items.abstract: SET binding protein 1 (SETBP1) is recurrently mutated in high-risk myeloid malignancies, including myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap disorders (MDS/MPNs) and is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Although SETBP1 mutations promote self-renewal and HOX-driven transcription in murine and cell line models, the epigenetic dependencies sustaining these programs in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a targetable dependency in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. Expression of SETBP1D886N enhanced growth and serial replating of human HSPCs and established a transcriptionally permissive chromatin state, with increased H3K4me3, H3K27ac and KMT2A occupancy at SETBP1-regulated loci. Integrated transcriptional and chromatin profiling defined a 94-gene SETBP1 regulome containing HOXA9, MEIS1, MECOM, and MYBand was enriched for transcriptional programs associated with KMT2A-rearranged, NUP98-HOXA9, and NPM1-mutant leukemias. CRISPR-Cas9 disruption revealed a functional requirement for KMT2A, but not for KMT2B or DOT1L in SETBP1D886N HSPCs. Strikingly, deletion of the KMT2A cofactor MEN1 phenocopied KMT2A loss. Disruption of either KMT2A or MEN1 suppressed SETBP1-driven proliferation and leukemogenic transcriptional programs, including leukemia stem cell-associated signatures. We next exploited this dependency pharmacologically. A KMT2A-MENIN inhibitor suppressed canonical SETBP1 target genes and abolished mutant SETBP1-driven serial replating while promoting hematopoietic differentiation and reducing H3K4me3 at leukemogenic loci, despite modest effects on short-term proliferation. Most importantly, three clinically relevant KMT2A-MENIN interaction inhibitors impaired clonogenic growth across primary SETBP1-mutant leukemia patient samples, while inducing myeloid differentiation and suppressing SETBP1 target gene expression. Together, these findings identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a key therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. The consistent activity of multiple MENIN inhibitors across a variety of SETBP1-mutant patient samples and cell models validates the KMT2A-MENIN interaction as an actionable vulnerability and provides a strong rationale for expanding MENIN-directed therapies to SETBP1-mutant myeloid malignancies.

items.title: Immune Age Acceleration Stratifies Survival in Multiple Myeloma Independent of Chronological Age and Clinical Fitness
items.abstract: Chronological age incompletely explains prognostic heterogeneity in multiple myeloma (MM), particularly among younger patients, whose clinical outcomes vary widely. Existing immune aging clocks are predominantly derived from peripheral blood expression data and thus incompletely reflect the aging of the bone marrow (BM) immune microenvironment in MM. To address this limitation, we developed BM immune aging clocks for ten immune and progenitor cell types trained on single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 1,260 healthy peripheral blood and BM samples and calibrated to BM. We then applied these clocks to BM single-cell profiles from 337 newly diagnosed MM patients enrolled in the CoMMpass study to derive a global immune age acceleration score. In patients younger than 70 at diagnosis, accelerated immune aging was independently associated with shorter overall survival (OS; HR = 2.24, p = 0.003) after adjustment for cytogenetic risk, transplant status, triplet therapy administration, chronological age, sex, performance status, and laboratory deficits, whereas chronological age was not predictive. Subsequent analyses identified CD4+ memory T cell aging as the strongest contributor to overall immune age acceleration and its association with shorter OS. Consistent with this, accelerated immune aging was characterized by terminal effector differentiation of memory T cells, TNF-/NF-{kappa}B-mediated inflammation, and increased lymphocyte-driven TNF, CCL3, and IFN-{gamma} signaling. However, inflammatory signaling alone did not account for survival differences. Longitudinally, changes in monocyte immune age acceleration at first progression were associated with shorter subsequent survival (HR = 3.06, p = 0.005). Together, these findings identify BM immune age acceleration as a prognostic measure of biological fitness in MM, distinct from chronological age and clinical frailty.

items.title: Subtype-specific autophagy profiles in Renal Cell Carcinoma
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway; Centre for Cancer Cell Reprogramming, Institute of Clin
items.abstract: Autophagy is a highly conserved cellular mechanism essential for recycling intracellular components and providing energy and maintaining cellular homeostasis. The role of autophagy in cancer is double sided, where it can suppress tumorigenesis by degrading damaged organelles and preventing chronic inflammation while supporting survival of existing tumor cells to survive during starvation and stress, and thus support tumor growth. The role of autophagy in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, remains insufficiently described. RCC originates from epithelial cells of the renal tubule and is divided into histological subtypes where clear cell RCC is the most common followed by papillary and chromophobe RCC, showing differences in morphology and molecular features. Recent studies of RCC suggest that mTORC1 and autophagy are involved in kidney cancer development and response to treatment, advocating the need to better understand the role of autophagy in RCC. To this end, we investigated autophagy markers by immunostaining, immunoblotting and quantitative PCR in biobanked fresh-frozen tissue samples of RCC tumor and matched normal tissue. Overall, we found reduced levels of LC3B and GABARAPL1 in clear cell RCC, in stark contrast to chromophobe RCC and benign oncocytoma. This suggests that autophagy levels differ between renal tumor subtypes, indicating that autophagy could play subtype-specific roles. In addition, autophagy modulating drug assays demonstrated autophagy dependencies in metastatic RCC cell line spheroids. This could provide new inroads for therapeutical approaches in RCC.

items.title: Cerulean Protein Tagging Enhances Immunogenicity and Osimertinib Response of Transplantable Murine EGFR Mutant Lung Cancer Cell Lines
items.corresponding_institution: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
items.abstract: Lung cancers bearing mutations in epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR) exhibit marked, but incomplete responses to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like osimertinib. We previously developed genetically-engineered mouse models (GEMMs) for EGFR exon 19 deletion (del19) and L860R (mouse equivalent of L858R). Sequences encoding mC3 cerulean fluorescent protein were included to mark emergent tumor cells. Orthotopic implantation of mEGFRdel19 cell lines into syngeneic C57BL/6J mice yielded tumors that were eliminated upon osimertinib therapy which is not typically observed in patients while mEGFR-L860R cell lines failed to establish tumors. Herein, mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R cell lines formed tumors in non-induced mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R GEMMs and green fluorescent protein-transgenic mice, supporting mC3-derived epitopes as mediators of immunoelimination. CRISPR-Cas9 mediated disruption of the mC3 cerulean sequence in established mEGFR cell lines yielded two independent mC3-deleted cell lines that formed orthotopic tumors and exhibited partial osimertinib responses. These studies provide a cautionary tale regarding use of fluorescent proteins in murine cancer models and reinforce host immunity as a participant in anti-tumor TKI responses initiated. These mC3-deleted cell lines serve as improved models to explore mechanisms of incomplete TKI response, acquired resistance and cancer cell interaction with the host immune microenvironment.

items.title: SHMT1 and SHMT2 inhibition disrupts metabolic adaptation in glioblastoma
items.corresponding_institution: Dr. Senckenberg Institute of Neurooncology, University Hospital Frankfurt, Goethe University, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
items.abstract: Glioblastoma cells adapt to hypoxia and nutrient restriction through metabolic reprogramming. Serine hydroxymethyltransferases 1 and 2 (SHMT1, SHMT2) channel serine-derived one carbon units into folate metabolism, linking biosynthesis, respiration and redox defence. Its contribution to tumour metabolic homeostasis and adaptation to hypoxia and nutrient restriction remains unclear. We combined dual pharmacological SHMT inhibition using (+)-SHIN1 in glioblastoma cell lines, including patient-derived glioma stem-like models, with stable SHMT2 knockdown in LNT-229 cells. Functional analyses assessed clonogenic survival, invasion, migration and susceptibility to metabolic stress. Bioenergetics were measured by extracellular flux analysis and oxygen depletion, redox state by NADPH/NADP; assay, and molecular responses by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and 13C6-glucose tracing and tandem mass tag proteomics. Formate supplementation tested the contribution of limited one-carbon availability, three-dimensional co-cultures with human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived embryoid bodies assessed tumour expansion, and in silico analyses of public glioblastoma datasets examined SHMT expression, regional distribution and associations with hypoxia-related genes. SHMT2 was enriched in hypoxic and perinecrotic tumour regions and correlated with hypoxia-inducible factor-1 target genes. SHMT inhibition impaired clonogenic growth, reduced invasion and migration, limited tumour expansion in co-culture, and sensitised cells to death under combined hypoxia and glucose restriction. Under normoxia, it increased respiration and estimates of glycolytic and oxidative ATP production. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition lowered intracellular and extracellular lactate and altered tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolite levels and 13C isotopologue signals. SHMT inhibition increased oxidative stress, reduced the NADPH/NADP; ratio in a cell line- and condition-dependent manner, and reduced extracellular formate accumulation. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition led to a depletion of glutathione. Formate supplementation most prominently restored invasion and partially reversed other antitumour effects of SHMT inhibition, with the extent of rescue varying between cell lines. Under combined stress, SHMT inhibition attenuated hypoxia-inducible factor-1-alpha; accumulation, an effect counteracted by formate supplementation. These findings link SHMT-dependent one-carbon metabolism to redox homeostasis, invasive behaviour and survival under metabolic stress in glioblastoma. SHMT inhibition increases respiratory activity under normoxia while compromising tolerance to combined oxygen and glucose restriction, identifying metabolic adaptation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in glioblastoma.

items.title: Novel selective CDK4-inhibitor ALK-13743: Functional determinants of response in ER+ breast cancer models
items.abstract: Background: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and CDK6 are central drivers of cell cycle progression in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer, and pharmacological inhibition of this pair has become a standard-of-care therapeutic strategy. However, currently approved CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib carry associated toxicities, including myelosuppression and other adverse effects which are associated with inhibition of CDK6 that limits tolerability and combinatorial strategies. Here we describe the preclinical characterization of ALK-13743, a novel, highly selective CDK4 inhibitor. Methods: ALK-13743 was synthesized and characterized biochemically for CDK4 selectivity. Anti-proliferative activity was assessed in wild-type (WT), RB1-deleted and CDK6-overexpressing isogenic ER+ breast cancer cell lines (MCF7, T47D) using live-cell fluorescence imaging. Impact on cell cycle progression was evaluated by immunoblotting. Combinatorial activity was assessed across a 307-drug library. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in T47D xenograft models. Results: ALK-13743 potently inhibited CDK4/Cyclin D1 with an IC50 of 33 nM and displayed selectivity over CDK6/Cyclin D3 (IC50, 99 nM), CDK2/Cyclin E1 (IC50, 1854 nM), and CDK1/Cyclin B1 (IC50, >10000 nM) in biochemical kinase assays. In cellular models, ALK-13743 demonstrated potent antiproliferative activity in CDK4-dependent ER+ breast cancer cells at nanomolar concentrations, while exhibiting limited inhibition in CDK6-dependent cell lines. ALK-13743 exhibited single-agent growth suppression and drug synergy with the selective estrogen receptor degrader giredestrant and PI3K pathway inhibitors but was entirely RB-dependent and blunted by CDK6 overexpression. Single-agent ALK-13743 treatment led to tumor regression in T47D xenografts in vivo. Conclusions: ALK-13743 is a potent, CDK4-selective inhibitor dependent upon RB for its antiproliferative profile in ER+ breast cancer models. Its favorable combinability with multiple clinically relevant targeted agents supports further development, particularly in combination regimens, and positions it as a differentiated CDK4-selective therapy for ER+ breast cancer.

items.title: The Neuroimmune Signature Underlying HPV Infection and Cervical Cancer Progression
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical and Toxicological Analyses, School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Sao Paulo (USP), Sao Paulo, Brazil
items.abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is the principal cause of cervical cancer, yet the multicellular signalling programmes that accompany disease progression remain incompletely defined. Here, we integrated Single cell RNA sequencing, independent microarray and bulk RNA-sequencing meta analyses, and TCGA CESC tumor data to characterize the neuroimmune transcriptional architecture of HPV associated cervical disease. Single cell profiling revealed progressive remodeling of epithelial, stromal, endothelial and immune compartments across HPV infection, high grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and cervical cancer. Although immune dysregulation predominated, lesion and tumor states showed coordinated enrichment of nervous system associated programs, including synapse organization, trans-synaptic signaling, axon development, neurogenesis and neurotransmitter-related signaling. These programs formed interconnected networks with cytokine production, leukocyte activation, chemotaxis, cell adhesion, apoptosis, and immune effector regulation. Cross-platform integration identified a recurrent 12-gene neuroimmune signature associated with tumor grade related transcriptional variation, including CXCL12, P2RY6, P2RX5 and TACR1. Ligand receptor inference further highlighted glutamatergic, adrenergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic and purinergic signaling circuits. Notably, these signals were distributed across immune, epithelial, stromal and endothelial populations rather than confined to a canonical neural cell compartment. P2RX5 showed the strongest association with advanced tumor grade, whereas P2RY6, P2RY11 and GABRP displayed cell type and stage dependent regulation. Together, our findings define cervical carcinogenesis as a distributed neuroimmune state in which HPV associated immune evasion converges with ectopic neurotransmission-related programs, revealing candidate biomarkers and potentially actionable signaling axes in the cervical tumor microenvironment.

items.title: Epithelial network percolation reshapes collective mechanochemical dynamics and modes of competitive cell elimination
items.corresponding_institution: Mechanobiology Institute, National University of Singapore, Singapore; Department of Physiology, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapo
items.abstract: Living tissues are active materials whose collective states depend on mechanochemical communication across connected cells. Yet tissues undergoing repair, ageing or tumorigenesis often contain intermingled cells with divergent states. How such heterogeneity alters tissue-scale communication, and whether cell competition can restore it, remains unclear. Here we track ERK activity, a dynamic readout and regulator of epithelial mechanochemical coupling, to ask how tissues recover from an aberrant state containing DNA-damaged cells. We show that damaged cells function as insulators, disrupting long-range ERK waves and partitioning control cells into disconnected clusters. As damaged cells are progressively eliminated by neighbouring control cells, fragmented clusters coalesce into a tissue-scale connected network through a percolation transition. Crossing this topological threshold restores collective ERK waves and coordinated cell motion, indicating recovery of tissue-scale mechanochemical order. Percolation also reshapes competitive elimination: before connectivity is restored, control cells remove damaged neighbours through actin-rich invasive protrusions; after percolation, connected control cells eliminate residual damaged cells by ERK-associated multicellular squeezing. Thus, cell competition actively reconfigures tissue topology to restore collective mechanochemical order.

items.title: RapidGLM: genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and eQTL analysis
items.abstract: Genome-scale differential expression, CRISPR screen and expression QTL analyses fit millions of count regressions and estimate p-values from billions of random draws. RapidGLM, a C++ library, makes both steps fast, with Newton fits specialized to count models and draws made in batches. Its DESeq2, edgeR, SCEPTRE and cis-QTL analyses agree with the reference tools and run 2.5-17.8 times faster on the same cores. On one compute node, a CRISPR screen's 28.0 million tests took SCEPTRE 11.6 hours and RapidGLM 44 minutes, or 2.8 hours with more accurate small p-values. RapidGLM is MIT-licensed, with C, Python, R and command-line interfaces.

items.title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
items.abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested as doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing studies. Given a source manuscript and a target dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, reports which findings transfer, and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

items.title: Saruparib recapitulates PARP-BRCA synthetic lethality with PARP1-trapping properties limiting its cytotoxicity
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Cell Growth and Tumor Regulation, Proteo-Science Center, Premier Institute for Advanced Studies, Ehime University, Toon, Ehime, 791-0295, Japan
items.abstract: The original concept of PARP synthetic lethality proposes that loss of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) activity selectively kills homologous recombination (HR)-deficient cells. However, clinically approved PARP1/2 inhibitors (PARPis) are used at exposures exceeding those required for catalytic inhibition. At these doses, PARP trapping is cytotoxic to HR-proficient cells and limits the therapeutic window in HR-deficient cancers. Saruparib has been developed as a PARP1-selective inhibitor to reduce PARP2-associated toxicity; yet its PARP1-trapping properties remain incompletely characterized. Here, we show that saruparib exhibits trapping properties distinct from those of conventional PARPis. It causes minimal cytotoxicity in HR-proficient cells and remains minimally toxic in XRCC1-deficient cells, which are highly sensitive to trapping-associated cytotoxicity induced by conventional PARPis. Although methyl methanesulfonate, which induces extensive base damage, increases saruparib-induced PARP1 trapping and cytotoxicity, the overall trapping-associated cytotoxic response is weaker than that induced by olaparib and shows little further dose-dependent increase once catalytic PARP1 inhibition is achieved. Biochemical measurements demonstrated that PARP1-DNA complexes formed in the presence of saruparib are less stable than those in the presence of olaparib or talazoparib. Notably, saruparib potently kills BRCA1-, BRCA2-, and PALB2-deficient cells at concentrations sufficient for near-maximal catalytic inhibition, without a corresponding increase in cytotoxicity in HR-proficient cells. Thus, saruparib combines potent HR-deficient-selective cytotoxicity with limited PARP1 trapping and associated toxicity. Consequently, saruparib closely recapitulates the PARP-BRCA synthetic lethality while sparing HR-proficient cells, providing a mechanistic framework for its rational clinical use.

items.title: LRCQ: phenome-wide heritability enrichment of genomic loci from GWAS summary statistics
items.abstract: Some genetic variants are associated with many traits, but a variant's GWAS statistics are also inflated by the effects of variants in LD with it and by confounding shared by all variants in a study. Existing measures of per-variant pleiotropy, such as counts of significant associations or multi-trait association tests, do not separate these sources. Stratified LD score regression separates them for one trait at a time and only through predefined annotations. We present LRCQ (LD score regression on {chi}2 across many GWAS), which estimates for each locus its phenome-wide heritability enrichment: the variance of its causal effects across a set of traits, relative to an average locus. LRCQ regresses squared Z-scores from 30 or more GWAS jointly on squared LD, with per-trait LDSC intercepts and heritabilities fitted in earlier stages. Its pooled least-squares solution has a closed form whose cost does not grow with the number of traits. Its standard errors account for sample overlap and genetic correlation between GWAS. Squared Z-scores identify enrichment at the resolution of LD clumps, not single SNPs, so LRCQ reports clump-level estimates ("omni-loci"). These estimates can be aggregated over any functional annotation or gene set chosen after the analysis. In simulations with real UK Biobank LD and 30 to 1,000 traits, LRCQ was unbiased for its clump-level estimand. When GWAS share samples its test statistics are strongly right-skewed: normal-reference p-values were up to 10-fold anti-conservative at P < 0.001. P-values matched to the exact third cumulant restored type-I error and FDR control, and matching the fourth cumulant as well kept the far tail within 1.6-fold of nominal down to P = 10-4. Score-type tests, which evaluate the variance under the null hypothesis, kept power at the most enriched loci. Model-based standard errors were calibrated once the enrichment estimates plugged into them kept the polygenic background. It ranked enriched loci better than mean {chi}2, LD-normalised {chi}2, multi-trait omnibus tests and significant-association counts in 13 of 16 scenarios. Its main vulnerability was a misspecified LDSC intercept. Applied to 444 Pan-UK Biobank European-ancestry GWAS, LRCQ found strongly non-uniform phenome-wide enrichment: the SD of true clump-mean enrichment was 8.3, against a genome mean of 1. It identified 661 omni-loci (921 LD clumps) at FDR 5%, including FTO, AXIN2, HBS1L-MYB, CST3, CELSR2-SORT1, PCSK9 and MC4R. These ranked only moderately with mean {chi}2 and poorly with counts of significant associations. Gene-level phenome-wide enrichment rose with loss-of-function constraint. Phenome-wide heritability was 3-5-fold enriched in coding, conserved, 5' UTR and promoter sequence, and depleted in repressed chromatin. LRCQ turns hundreds of biobank GWAS into an LD-corrected map of where phenome-wide genetic variance lies, and complements its companion method LRCP, which estimates genetic-effect correlations between loci.

items.title: LRCP: identifying functionally related SNPs and genes from phenome-wide genetic-effect correlations using GWAS summary statistics
items.abstract: Genetic correlation describes which traits share genetic causes. The transposed question, which variants act alike across the phenome, has no comparable estimator, although it points directly to shared genes, pathways and regulators. Correlations of GWAS Z scores between variants across many traits are easy to compute, but they are confounded by linkage disequilibrium (LD) and, for any pair of variants, by sample overlap and genetic correlation among the GWAS. We show that in 452 Pan-UK Biobank GWAS the effective number of independent traits is only 58, and that naive tests reject 51-70% of null pairs of distal variants. We introduce LRCP (likelihood and regression on cross-products of Z scores), which estimates the phenome-wide genetic-effect correlation{rho} between SNPs by regressing Z-score cross-products on LD cross components, using per-SNP heritability enrichment from the companion method LRCQ and LDSC-derived plug-ins. For variants in different LD blocks the estimator has a closed form, and its standard errors account exactly for the dependence among GWAS. In simulations LRCP is unbiased (absolute bias at most 0.03), its 95% intervals cover 93-98%, and its type-I error is 5.0-5.7%, whereas naive correlations are attenuated by 41-64% and reject up to 51% of null pairs. In Pan-UK Biobank, LRCP recovers the expected signs among PCSK9, LDLR and APOB variants and estimates{rho} = 0.90 between the TP53 polyadenylation variant rs78378222 and MDM2 rs3730556, whose Z scores correlate at r = 0.67 across traits (conditional bootstrap P = 0.015), although this correlation lies along a shared body-size and red-cell trait axis. Single variant pairs are near the resolution of current biobanks, with precision limited by the number of genetically distinct traits. Genome-wide, among 1,799 strongly enriched LD clumps (1.61 million distal pairs), a conditional test finds 437 pairs at FDR 5%, where naive correlation flags 1.1 million. Simulating the whole screen under the null shows that this test is conservative and that the 386 strongest links (P < 10-5) lie beyond every one of 322 million simulated null statistics. Linked genes share GO biological processes 1.9 times more often than random pairs of enriched loci. The links form 14 modules that match known biology, among them platelet and red-cell production, lipoprotein metabolism (PCSK9, LDLR, APOB, CETP, LPL), myeloid differentiation (IRF8, ITGA4), bone density (WNT16), pigmentation (HERC2, SLC45A2), alkaline phosphatase (ALPL, GPLD1) and IL-6 signalling (IL6R, CRP). Most modules act within one trait domain, where LRCP shows shared trait profiles rather than a tested shared mechanism. Once LD and the dependence among GWAS are modelled, phenome-wide summary statistics can identify functionally related variants and genes.

items.title: YAP1-induced super-enhancer rewiring mediates gene-environment-driven malignant reprogramming and metastatic ecosystem formation in head and neck cancer
items.corresponding_institution: National Hospital Organization Kyushu Cancer Center
items.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterized by frequent TP53 mutations, which are insufficient for tumorigenesis and largely undruggable, underscoring the need to define epigenetic mechanisms driving cancer evolution. Here we show that TP53 mutation facilitates YAP1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming, driving epigenetic tumor evolution by hijacking tissue-regenerative programs. Integrated multi-omics analyses of mouse models and multiregional human HNSCC samples reveal that global chromatin architecture remains largely stable during progression, whereas YAP1 dynamically redistributes to newly formed super-enhancers accompanied by enhancer DNA hypomethylation. Mechanistically, YAP1 establishes an IL6-dependent feedforward loop and cooperates with stage-specific transcription factors, including FOXM1, DeltaNp63, and PITX2. The YAP1-PITX2 axis promotes partial EMT, cancer-associated fibroblast activation, and lymph node metastasis, resulting in a fibrotic and immunosuppressive metastatic ecosystem. These findings identify a YAP1-driven epigenetic circuit as a central hub linking environmental stress to malignant reprogramming and highlight a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HNSCC.

items.title: MUC4 regulatory-region methylation is remodeled during breast cancer progression and metastasis
items.corresponding_institution: University of California Davis School of Medicine
items.abstract: Background Mucin-4 (MUC4) contributes to tumor cell survival and metastatic behavior, but its expression in breast cancer is unusual; previous studies have demonstrated that MUC4 levels are reduced in primary tumors relative to normal epithelium but are partially restored in metastatic lesions. Because DNA methylation is known to regulate MUC4 gene expression in cultured cancer cells, we investigated whether methylation of the MUC4 regulatory region changes across breast cancer progression. Results Analysis of the TCGA-BRCA database revealed that primary breast tumors exhibit increased methylation at CpG sites within the MUC4 regulatory region relative to normal breast tissue, and methylation at key sites is inversely associated with MUC4 transcript abundance. Moreover, DNA methyltransferase inhibition with 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine alters MUC4 expression in several breast cancer cell lines. Finally, targeted bisulfite sequencing analysis of an independent cohort of normal breast, primary breast tumor, and metastatic breast cancer specimens revealed that MUC4 in primary tumors is significantly more methylated than in normal breast tissue at all 11 CpG sites examined. Metastatic specimens in this cohort generally display lower methylation than primary tumors and an intermediate methylation profile between normal and primary tissue. Conclusions Taken together, our findings support MUC4 regulatory region methylation as a contributor to stage-dependent MUC4 regulation.

items.title: Branched-Chain α-Keto Acid Mitochondrial Uptake Regulates Fatty Acid Metabolism in Adipose Tissue
items.abstract: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are essential amino acids and their homeostasis is tightly regulated by mostly mitochondrial localized catabolic activities where branched-chain -keto acids (BCKAs) are the first-step downstream products. BCAAs and BCKAs are both readily detected in circulation, necessitating targeted transporters for their uptake across cellular and mitochondrial membranes. Although mitochondrial transporter for BCAA uptake has been identified, the molecular entity for BCKAs mitochondrial uptake remains unknown. In adult mice, we measured circulating BCAA and BCKAs under feeding and fasting status, and found circulating BCKAs were markedly elevated during fasting while BCAAs levels remained constant. By integrating genetic association analysis in human and multi-tissue nutrient-responsive transcriptomic profiling in mice, we identified SLC25A35 as a candidate mitochondrial transporter highly associated with BCKA homeostasis. SLC25A35 expression was highly enriched in brown adipocytes. Genetic inactivation of SLC25A35 in mice specifically blunted BCKA mitochondria uptake and downstream catabolism without significant impact on BCAA homeostasis, as demonstrated by targeted metabolic profiling and isotope tracing in intact animals, in isolated primary adipocytes and in purified mitochondria. SLC25A35 expression directly promoted mitochondrial BCKA uptake, with a preference for KIC and KMV over KIV. Importantly, SLC25A35 mediated BCKA uptake and catabolism was independent from SLC25A44 mediated BCAA mitochondrial transport, and the BCKA specificity for SLC35A35 was further evaluated by structure-guided identification and mutagenesis based validation for conserved potential BCKA interacting residues in SLC25A35 transmembrane domains. Functionally, SLC25A35 expression enhanced lipogenesis by supporting fatty acid incorporation of BCKA-derived carbon and lipogenic gene expression, independent from mitochondrial production of PEP. During cold exposure, SLC25A35-deficient mice exhibited reduced mitochondrial respiratory activity in brown adipose tissue , depletion of short- and long-chain acylcarnitine species, and attenuated cold-responsive metabolic signalling. Together, these findings identify SLC25A35 as a nutrient-responsive mitochondrial BCKA transporter that reveal a previously unrecognized BCKA specific contribution to adipocyte lipid metabolism and thermogenic adaptation.

items.title: Fragment anchoring for metabolite annotation beyond whole-spectrum similarity
items.abstract: Many untargeted metabolomics features remain unannotated, and chemically related metabolites can have dissimilar tandem mass spectra. We present ANCHor, a framework for interpreting features of interest using shared fragment evidence. ANCHor selects fragments of a feature that recur among similar atlas spectra but are rare in background spectra, then evaluates matching experimental features using mass differences and transformation rules. Using 1,021 authentic standards as features of interest, ANCHor generated at least one anchor for 76.9%. We tested whether L-methionine anchors retain related spectra despite low overall similarity. Of 166 structurally related spectra, ANCHor retained 147, including 93 with modified cosine similarity <0.70 to L-methionine. In mycotoxin-treated hepatic spheroids, ANCHor prioritized putative transformation products, including low-similarity candidates. For library-unmatched fecal features in alcohol-associated liver disease, ANCHor found annotated references that guided identification of N1,N12-diacetylspermine, confirmed with an authentic standard, and supported a tryptophan-pyruvate product hypothesis with a reaction-generated reference. ANCHor thus supports testable structural hypotheses for library-unmatched features within atlas coverage.

items.title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
items.abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

items.title: Zhx2 expression in the mouse brain
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Addiction Genetics, Department of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Sciences and Center for Drug Discovery, Northeastern University, Boston, MA USA
items.abstract: Prescription opioids like oxycodone (OXY; the active component in OxyContin) continue to drive the ongoing opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic due to their widespread prescription and distribution.
