Genetic factors influencing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of opioids can have profound impacts on drug response and, in turn, influence risk for OUD. We previously used quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and gene validation to identify zinc-finger homeobox 2 (Zhx2) loss-of-function as a quantitative trait gene and mechanism underlying increased brain concentration of oxymorphone (OMOR) following systemic administration of OXY in BALB/cJ females that was linked to increased OXY reward. To test whether we could rescue the behavioral phenotype, we overexpressed Zhx2 in the brain via retro-orbital injection of a brain-specific adeno-associated virus (AAV). We observed restricted Zhx2 expression (especially females), with more widespread expression in males. Consequently, we did not observe any significant effect of brain Zhx2 overexpression on OXY reward as measured via conditioned place preference (CPP). However, Zhx2 overexpression did protect against OXY-induced weight loss in females following a high-dose OXY regimen. Despite the effect on weight loss, Zhx2 overexpression had no effect on spontaneous or naloxone-precipitated withdrawal behaviors. We then examined native Zhx2 protein expression in the brains of the BALB/cByJ substrain (showing wild-type levels of Zhx2 expression) via immunohistochemical co-localization and found that Zhx2 is mainly expressed in neurons located in key reward, motivational, and emotion-related regions such as the hippocampus (HPC), amygdala, striatum (Str), and cerebellum. To summarize, Zhx2 overexpression via retro-orbital AAV administration was quite limited, yet had significant effects on opioid-induced weight loss. Furthermore, for the first time, we provide anatomical visualization of Zhx2 expression at the protein level in neurons vs. glia throughout multiple brain regions.

items.title: Investigating the effect of acute consumption of kiwifruit on cognitive function using functional MRI
items.abstract: Objectives: Acute nutritional interventions may modulate cognitive function and underlying brain activity. This study investigated the impact of consuming three kiwifruit varieties - green (Zespri Green), gold (Zespri SunGold), and red (Zespri RubyRed) - on cognitive performance and brain activation using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Methods: Fourteen healthy participants completed a randomized, repeated-measures study involving four MRI sessions following consumption of each kiwifruit type and a maltodextrin control. Cognitive function was assessed using an N-back working memory task during fMRI acquisition. Behavioural performance, psychometric measures (mood, fatigue, appetite), and blood biomarkers (vitamin C) were also collected. Results: Kiwifruit consumption significantly increased plasma vitamin C levels relative to control, with peak concentrations observed at 100 minutes post-consumption. Behaviourally, task difficulty increased with N-back load, while psychometric measures indicated greater positive affect following kiwifruit compared to control. fMRI results showed that the maltodextrin condition elicited broader brain activation, suggesting reduced neural efficiency. In contrast, kiwifruit -particularly the red variety - showed enhanced differentiation between low and high cognitive load (2-back vs. 0-back), with increased activation in regions associated with working memory and cognitive control. Conclusions: These findings suggest that acute kiwifruit consumption may enhance cognitive efficiency and modulate brain responses, with effects varying by kiwifruit cultivar.

items.title: Predicting conformational changes induced by biomolecular interactions
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Chemistry; Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI; Department of AX; InnoCORE AI-CRED Institute, KAIST, Republic of Korea; HITS Inc., Seoul, Republic o
items.abstract: Biomolecular interactions trigger structural changes of protein complexes essential for cellular signaling, regulation, and drug action. Modern co-folding models can now generate detailed structures of multi-component complexes directly from sequence. However, recent evaluations reveal that they frequently fail to capture specific conformational states induced by a ligand or partner. Here, we show that explicitly modeling the structural transition from an unbound to a bound state, rather than generating the bound complex alone, better resolves these interaction-induced states. Our generative learning framework, K-Fold, transforms independently predicted unbound component priors into an assembled complex through an ultrafast diffusion bridge, operating entirely without multiple sequence alignments. By eliminating co-evolutionary dependencies, K-Fold accurately recovers non-coevolved interfaces in antibody-antigen and targeted-degrader complexes, as well as ligand-directed regulatory states in GPCRs and kinases. Furthermore, by coupling this diffusion bridge with diverse monomeric equilibrium ensembles, K-Fold provides a computationally tractable foundation for sampling complex multi-state landscapes without retraining. These results demonstrate that formulating molecular assembly as an explicit structural transition moves structure prediction beyond static geometries toward capturing biomolecular dynamics.

items.title: Semaglutide quiets "food noise" in mice by impairing the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose
items.abstract: Semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists are transforming obesity treatment, and patients often describe a quieting of intrusive food thoughts that motivate overconsumption of ultra-palatable foods, referred to as "food noise," yet it remains unclear which components of feeding behavior they act upon. Here, we designed a battery of behavioral tasks that separate the perceptual, hedonic, and motivational components of glucose intake in mice. Semaglutide impaired sweet taste categorization (in a psychophysical task) and induced conditioned taste avoidance not aversion, and thus left palatability intact. Its largest effect, however, was on motivation: it selectively disrupted the active pursuit of glucose and, to a lesser extent, lipids, sparing passive intake. In a novel lick-triggered taste alternation task, two fixed sippers delivered either glucose or a second tastant (e.g., saccharin or lipids), with the tastants swapping positions after a set number of licks. This design separated effortless consumption, when the swap brought glucose directly to the mouse (passive hit), from effortful pursuit requiring crossing to the opposite sipper (active hit). A single dose of semaglutide left passive hits intact, but markedly reduced active hits: mice readily exploited glucose that came to them, yet often failed to go after it. As the drug's effect waned, mice regained body weight by selectively overconsuming standard chow over glucose, and glucose over lipids, a shift in diet choice that persisted through the end of the experiment. Thus, semaglutide impairs the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose, providing (in mice) a behavioral correlate of the quieting of "food noise" reported by patients.

items.title: Tonic dopamine regulates cell-type-specific PKA activity and motivated behavior
items.corresponding_institution: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Harvard Medical School
items.abstract: Dopamine in the striatum fluctuates on fast ``phasic`` and slow ``tonic`` timescales. Although disruptions in tonic dopamine have been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disease, the effect of slow, minutes-long fluctuations in dopamine on neuronal activity and behavior remain unknown. Here we use two-color fluorescence lifetime photometry at high temporal resolution (FLIPR) and calibrated optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the impact of tonic dopamine on motivated behavior and downstream signaling in vivo. We establish a method for tracking tonic dopamine using FLIPR and determine that dopamine release fluctuates across short (100s of milliseconds) and long (10s of minutes) timescales. We find that dopamine type 1 (D1R) and type 2 (D2R) receptor expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are differentially affected by changes in tonic dopamine in vivo, confirming long-standing hypothesis on tonic dopamine function in the striatum. Finally, we show that accumbal tonic dopamine levels predict and causally mediate an animal`s motivation to work for reward by regulating the rate of reward-motivated actions and engagement in a progressive ratio task. Altogether, we show that tonic dopamine affects downstream signaling and motivated behavior, and establish a new set of methods that allows for careful capture and manipulation of tonic dopamine in vivo.

items.title: Early life stress reduces prefrontal dendritic spine density in adult male mice
items.corresponding_institution: SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University and New York University
items.abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is a major risk factor for anxiety, depression and substance use disorders later in life, and it is thought to act in part by changing how emotion-regulating circuits develop. The prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices exert top-down control over the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and this circuit is still maturing during early postnatal life. Stress in adulthood removes dendritic spines from prefrontal neurons, but it is less clear whether ELS causes lasting spine changes across this circuit, and the IL in particular has rarely been studied. Here, we asked whether ELS alters dendritic spine density in the PL, IL and BLA of adult male mice. From postnatal day (PND) 10 to 17, ELS pups were separated from the dam for 3 h per day and individually isolated from their littermates, and their home cage had reduced nesting material until PND21. Control pups were separated together with their littermates for only 15 min per day and kept standard nesting. In adulthood, brains were processed for Golgi-Cox staining, and spines were counted on proximal apical and basal dendrites of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the PL and IL, and on dendrites of principal neurons in the BLA. ELS reduced spine density by approximately 30% in the IL and PL dendrites, with the largest losses concentrated on proximal apical dendrites. The BLA showed a smaller reduction of about 12%. These preliminary findings suggest that ELS leads to an important and lasting loss of dendritic spines in prefrontal regions that regulate emotional responses.

items.title: Dissociated network and cellular remodeling in the hippocampal-cortical circuit after induction of neuronal hyperexcitability
items.abstract: Neuronal hyperexcitability (NHE) can leave lasting consequences in neuronal circuits. It is often assumed that hyperexcitable neurons give rise to hyperactive networks. Here we asked how a single injection of kainic acid, which induces NHE without seizures, reshapes the hippocampal-cortical circuit at the cellular and network levels two months later. Using high-density microelectrode arrays in acute slices, we found a long-lasting reduction in spontaneous firing and bursting across the hippocampal regions, a lower proportion of active electrodes throughout the circuit, and weaker coupling from CA1 to the entorhinal cortex. In contrast, whole-cell recordings revealed region- and cell-type-specific changes in intrinsic excitability. CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons and CA3 interneurons exhibited increased evoked firing, whereas CA1 interneurons exhibited reduced evoked firing. Deep-layer entorhinal neurons, however, received less excitatory synaptic input and fired less. Thus, network and cellular alterations were dissociated after NHE. Finally, a pharmacological challenge with the GluK1 agonist ATPA revealed region-specific changes in network responsiveness, with a blunted response in CA3 and enhanced response in the non-entorhinal cortex, with no differences in DG, CA1 or entorhinal cortex. These findings suggest that, after the induction of NHE, region- and cell-type-specific neuronal remodeling coexists with reduced network activity ex vivo, and that the state of the circuit cannot be inferred from the properties of its individual neurons.

items.title: The mechanical nature of injury shapes the composition and temporal dynamics of inflammation after traumatic spinal cord injury
items.abstract: The pathophysiology of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex, evolving process that begins with a mechanical trauma. Progressive secondary damage then occurs, in which neuroinflammation plays a pivotal role. Much has been learned about the persistent inflammatory response during the chronic phase of SCI. However, variations in lesion models, animal species, strains, and the post-lesion intervals investigated make it difficult to conclude on how inflammation contributes to recovery or to exacerbation of damage. Here, we systematically compared two preclinical rat models of thoracic SCI: contusion and bilateral dorsal hemisection (bDH), that produce severe injuries leading to comparable initial locomotor deficits. We present a detailed analysis of neuroinflammatory temporal dynamics from acute (1-7 days), subacute (14 days), and chronic stages (> 4 weeks). The two models shared some inflammatory patterns, but specific cellular and molecular responses differed in magnitude, composition, and temporal evolution. These signature inflammatory dynamics were associated with differences in endogenous axonal plasticity, astroglial remodeling and progressive lesion maturation, and with distinct functional recovery rates. As the lesion gradually became chronic, inflammatory activity was remodeled, but persisted. These results reveal the interplay between the mechanical cause of SCI, the corresponding immune response, and the ensuing tissue remodeling processes. They highlight the importance of injury context and subsequent evolution. We discuss them as contributions to our understanding of the physiopathology of spinal cord lesions, with the broader goal of designing therapeutic strategies aiming to appropriately modulate inflammation

items.title: Targeting Heparan Sulfate 3-O-Sulfation Enhances Acetylcholine Receptor Clustering and Stabilizes Neuromuscular Junctions in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
items.corresponding_institution: Inserm, IMRB U955, Universite Paris Est Creteil (UPEC)
items.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe neuromuscular disease caused by dystrophin deficiency, leading to progressive muscle degeneration and neuromuscular junction (NMJ) instability. Using rat models of DMD, we identified a dysregulation in heparan sulfate (HS) biosynthesis at the NMJ, characterized by reduced expression of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 genes that encode sulfotransferases required for the production of rare 3-O-sulfated heparan sulfate (3S-HS) forms. These genes act synergistically to enhance agrin signaling: their co-expression in myotubes potentiates acetylcholine receptor clustering, and HSPG mimics bearing tetrasulfated 3-O-sulfated motifs reproduce this effect and promote Agrin-LRP4 interaction. In DMD rats, muscle co-transduction of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 prevents NMJ fragmentation and improves muscle strength. These findings identify 3S-HSs as novel regulators of NMJ stability and support HS modulation as a complementary therapeutic strategy in DMD.

items.title: Constructing value on the fly from episodic memory supports flexible decision-making
items.abstract: Value-based decisions often require people to flexibly draw on and combine information from past experiences to evaluate novel stimuli and adapt to changing demands. Although numerous studies have highlighted the involvement of episodic memory in value-based decision-making, whether and how a common episodic mechanism can support diverse decision-making scenarios remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce GENESIS-Value, a computational framework that constructs value on the fly by retrieving and integrating episodic memories, rather than relying on stable, precomputed value representations. The model combines generative stimulus representations with a flexible query-key-value retrieval mechanism, allowing the same memory store to support different valuation and choice strategies. Across five simulations, we demonstrate that GENESIS-Value can use episodic sampling to reconstruct the values of experienced stimuli, generalize to novel stimuli based on shared features, estimate feature values, guide both individual and sequential choices, and select among multiple offers involving different rewards and levels of risk. We further show that retrieval can be guided by stimulus features, temporal proximity, reminders, and reward outcomes, as well as combinations of these factors, enabling adaptation to different decision demands without requiring separate value functions. The model also captures qualitative behavioral signatures reported in empirical studies of episodic decision-making. Together, these findings establish a unified computational account of how episodic retrieval can support diverse forms of value-based inference and choice. Rather than replacing stable value representations, episodic retrieval may provide a complementary mechanism that allows decision-makers to flexibly address a variety of choice scenarios by reconstructing the value of available options on the fly.

items.title: Development of a high-throughput protein array to discover selective dsRNA binding domain interactions
items.corresponding_institution: University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center
items.abstract: Endogenous double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) function as signal transduction molecules through interactions with host proteins. These interactions can induce signaling cascades implicated in normal homeostasis and diseases such as cancer. Therefore, the discovery of interactions between dsRNAs and dsRNA binding proteins (dsRBPs) is critical for comprehensive elucidation of signal transduction cascades. Discovery of dsRNA-dsRBP interactions remains hindered due to technical limitations that can include a lack of reliable reagents to enrich a given dsRBP or enrichment techniques that cannot identify direct dsRNA-dsRBP binding. As an alternative, we report the development of protein domain arrays to enable high-throughput discovery of direct interactions between dsRNAs and dsRBP reader domains. We establish a modular antibody-independent approach coined dsRBP-seq to identify putative dsRNAs. Validated dsRNAs are subsequently used to probe dsRBP domain arrays to discover multiple dsRNA binding domains that bind the same dsRNA. The establishment and application of this new technical approach reveals a domain-specific interaction of the dsRNA transcript encoding 26S proteasome complex subunit, Sem1, that binds with double-stranded RNA binding motif 3 of Staufen Double-Stranded RNA Binding Protein 2 (STAU2). Altogether, our workflow establishes a high-throughput approach to discover direct dsRNA-dsRBP interactions and the protein domains required for dsRNA binding.

items.title: Quantum-assisted genomic prediction of blast resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) using SNP and haplotype representations
items.abstract: Rice blast caused by Magnaporthe oryzae threatens rice production, and genomic prediction may accelerate identification of resistant germplasm. We evaluated classical machine-learning and simulated quantum-kernel models for binary and three-class prediction of leaf blast (BL) and panicle blast (PB) resistance in 204 rice accessions with 2,120 repeated phenotypic observations. Models used 328,597 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), 104,068 phased haplotypes, or 49,451 unphased haplotypes. Binary prediction outperformed three-class prediction. The highest binary macro-F1 scores were 0.87 for BL and 0.73 for PB. Phased and unphased haplotypes reduced predictor dimensionality by 68.3% and 85.0%, respectively, while retaining broadly comparable performance. Quantum support vector classification achieved competitive results in selected binary tasks but did not consistently exceed the strongest classical models. These findings establish a benchmark for SNP- and haplotype-based prediction of rice blast resistance and for evaluation of quantum machine learning in crop genomics.

items.title: Spatial and epigenetic programs underlie heterogeneous cellular senescence in the aging liver
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego School of Medicine, La Jolla, CA, USA; Center for Epigenomics, University of
items.abstract: Aging is a complex biological process leading to tissue dysfunction, and driven in part by progressive epigenetic drift, widespread transcriptional dysregulation and cellular senescence. Senescent cells (SnCs) accumulate across tissues in a heterogeneous and cell type-specific manner, yet their molecular signatures and spatial organization within native tissue have not been systematically mapped. Here we combined single-nucleus transcriptomic, epigenomic, three-dimensional (3D) genome and spatial profiling to systematically characterize aging of the mouse liver and associated cellular senescence. Aging was marked by hepatocyte loss, immune cell expansion, erosion of repressive H3K9me3 heterochromatin, alteration of 3D genome organization, and activation of stress-response pathways known to promote senescence. Age-associated SnCs were spatially colocalized within discrete inflammatory microenvironments termed SenSpots. Different SenSpots were dominated by distinct hepatocyte senescence states (senotypes), driven by unique transcription factors, and exhibited distinct lobular zonation. Single-cell DNA methylation profiling revealed a subset of immune cells in aged livers with loss of DNA methylation at constitutive heterochromatin and elevated senescence signatures. AAV-mediated, p21-promoter driven Stat1 deletion in the aged liver selectively suppressed interferon-responsive senescence programs while pharmacological inhibition of MDM2 attenuated senescence-associated inflammatory signatures. Together, these findings reveal that hepatic senescence is not a uniform state but a set of diverse epigenetically reprogrammed, spatially organized, and pharmacologically modifiable inflammatory niches.

items.title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
items.abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

items.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy for Quantitative Prediction of Multicomponent Mixtures
items.corresponding_institution: Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering, Texas A & M University, College Station, Texas, United States
items.abstract: Machine Learning (ML)-assisted Raman spectroscopy that can efficiently analyze molecularly specific fingerprints is well suited for quantitative analysis of complex chemical mixtures. However, developing accurate predictive ML models for multicomponent systems remains difficult because collecting sufficient experimental calibration data is slow, expensive, and limited. In this work, we present a ML-assisted Raman spectroscopy framework for predicting the quantitative composition of multicomponent lipid mixtures (consisting of 15 lipids). To reduce the experimental burden of generating extensive multicomponent spectral datasets, we computationally constructed a large spectral library using experimentally measured pure-component Raman spectra from 15 lipids, including triglycerides, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, and fatty acid methyl and ethyl esters. Mixture compositions were sampled across a constrained compositional space and used to generate training spectra from weighted combinations of the pure component spectra. Experimentally prepared mixtures were then used to evaluate the model under real measurement conditions. To reduce the mismatch between library-generated spectra and experimental mixture spectra, a linear correction strategy was applied to account for systematic spectral differences caused by mixing effects, intermolecular interactions, and measurement variability. The corrected experimental spectra were then used for concentration prediction with an uncertainty-aware workflow. The compositions of the 15 lipid mixtures were successfully predicted using the ML model trained solely on a simulated dataset, achieving R^2 values exceeding 0.95 for each lipid. By combining scalable, library-based model training with experimental validation on physical multicomponent mixtures, this approach minimizes the need for exhaustive calibration datasets while maintaining high quantitative accuracy. The proposed framework offers a practical path for quantitative Raman analysis of chemical mixtures and can easily be extended to quality control applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and chemical industries.

items.title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
items.abstract: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

items.title: Prediction and Dissection of Nitrogenase Activity Based on Protein Sequences using Dual Descriptor
items.abstract: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, but its activity differs markedly among natural sequences, and conventional wet-laboratory screening suffers from low throughput and long turnaround times. Existing computational methods have partially alleviated this bottleneck, yet most of them rely on protein embeddings obtained from protein language models together with features such as gene expression, and their interpretability analyses mostly stop at the level of feature contribution. Here we present CarmnaDD, a purely sequence-driven framework built on the dual descriptor (DD): two learnable components, the composition weight map (CWM) and the position weight function (PWF), jointly generate a position-resolved description N(k), so that activity can be predicted without any prior knowledge beyond the sequence. On the same dataset used by Carmna, CarmnaDD attains R2 = 0.60 for regression and AUC = 0.94 and F1 = 0.86 for classification, better than our previous Carmna, which integrates multiple features. Interpretability analysis shows that the amplitude of the periodic terms of the PWF decreases as the rank increases, indicating that the positional encoding strategy adapts to the rank; the high-weight 3-mer fragments in the CWM are significantly enriched in polar uncharged residues, which corroborates the SHAP-based conclusion of Carmna; sliding-window scanning identifies fragments significantly associated with activity (FDR < 0.05), and the strongest window displays a D-X-E pattern with conserved flanks and a polymorphic center, sequences carrying R at the central position showing the highest activity; conservation is significantly negatively correlated ({rho} = -0.30) with description intensity. Mapping the key windows onto the protein structure shows that four highly correlated windows converge on the nucleotide-binding interface and the conformational-transmission/protein-docking interface of NifH. These results provide a purely sequence-based framework for nitrogenase activity prediction that balances performance and interpretability.

items.title: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produces synergistic anti-tumour activity across preclinical glioblastoma models
items.abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains difficult to treat because of tumour heterogeneity and the limited activity of single-target therapies. Our previous phenotypic drug screen identified JAK2/STAT3 signalling and HSP90-dependent protein homeostasis as pharmacological vulnerabilities. We investigated whether combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition could produce broader anti-tumour activity across GBM models. Methods: Multiple JAK2 and HSP90 inhibitors were tested alone and in combination across 2- and 3-dimensional patient-derived GBM stem cell models. Drug interactions were quantified using the zero-interaction potency (ZIP) synergy model. Mechanistic studies included RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, western blotting, immunofluorescence and FUCCI live-cell imaging. Activity was also assessed in cerebral organoid GBM co-cultures, non-malignant human neural and glial cells and orthotopic GBM xenografts. Results: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produced synergistic interactions in 12 of the 13 GBM cell lines tested, using multiple structurally distinct inhibitor pairs. Gandotinib and NMS-E973 were selected for further mechanistic studies, where the combination reduced spheroid growth and increased caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage. Combination treatment was associated with G2/M accumulation, altered mitotic regulation, abnormal chromosome and spindle organisation, and increased gamma-H2AX signalling. Anti-tumour combination activity was maintained in cerebral organoid co-cultures, where tumour burden was reduced as assessed by imaging, histological and luciferase-based measurements, while the drug combination had relatively limited effects on non-malignant human neural and glial cell types tested over the same concentration range. In vivo, combined Pacritinib and NMS-E973 treatment significantly reduced tumour burden in orthotopic G7 xenografts compared with vehicle or either single agent. Conclusions: JAK2/HSP90 co-inhibition produces reproducible anti-tumour activity across heterogeneous GBM models and disrupts cell-cycle and mitotic progression. These findings support further evaluation of this combination strategy in GBM.

items.title: Low serine-glycine-one-carbon pathway activity defines purine salvage dependence in neuroblastoma
items.corresponding_institution: University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL
items.abstract: MYCN amplification promotes serine-glycine-one-carbon (SGOC) metabolism in neuroblastoma, creating an intrinsic difference in SGOC activity between MYCNamplified and non-MYCN-amplified high-risk tumors. This metabolic distinction provides a model to investigate how SGOC activity shapes purine metabolism. Here, we show that non-MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines exhibit lower SGOC pathway activity and are more resistant to pharmacologic suppression of SGOC metabolism by SHMT inhibition under serine- and glycine-deprived conditions. Stable-isotope tracing revealed that non-MYCN-amplified cells exhibited lower contribution of serine-derived glycine and one-carbon units to de novo purine synthesis but elevated basal hypoxanthine and adenine salvage. These cells also showed greater preservation of adenylate pools during SHMT inhibition. Genetic depletion of APRT or HPRT1 preferentially impaired proliferation of non-MYCN-amplified cells, demonstrating increased salvage dependence. SHMT inhibition increased purine salvage, providing additional evidence that suppression of SGOC metabolism shifts purine production toward salvage. We also identify methionine salvage as an endogenous source of adenine that supports proliferation during SHMT inhibition through an MTAP-adenine-APRT axis. Together, these findings establish SGOC pathway activity as an intrinsic determinant of whether cells preferentially rely on de novo purine synthesis or purine salvage and identify salvage dependence as a potential therapeutic vulnerability of low-SGOC tumors.

items.title: Temporal blood sampling improves parameter recovery in a model of enterohepatic bile acid circulation using surrogate-accelerated Bayesian inference
items.abstract: Bile acids (BAs) are essential signaling molecules whose enterohepatic circulation (EHC) is disrupted across hepatobiliary disorders. Despite their potential as biomarkers, clinical utility is limited by high inter-individual variability, the inability of accessible peripheral blood to reflect true hepatic exposure, and the difficulty of directly measuring key physiological parameters governing the EHC. While mechanistic models can infer inaccessible hepatic profiles and patient-specific parameters from peripheral blood, personalizing them is computationally prohibitive due to multiscale dynamics causing numerical stiffness and the thousands of evaluations required for Bayesian inference. To overcome this, we developed an accelerated Bayesian inference pipeline combining timescale model reduction with neural network surrogates. Eigenvector participation factor analysis of a human EHC model revealed that rapid portal vein and hepatic sinusoidal transport drive stiffness. Applying the quasi-steady state approximation to these fast variables reduced integration times by over 97% with an integrated relative error 90% of the identifiability of five time points. Furthermore, the framework captured EHC compensatory dynamics, revealing a persistent positive correlation between intestinal transit and absorption. By making stiff EHC models tractable, our framework guides clinical study design and enables minimally invasive, mechanistic characterization of BA dysregulation, advancing our mechanistic understanding and personalized diagnosis of hepatobiliary diseases.

items.title: NeuroImgAgent: a multi-agent platform for cross-species fMRI analysis with evidence-gated quality control
items.corresponding_institution: State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System, Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen 518055, China
items.abstract: Cross-species functional MRI analysis requires coordinating specialized workflows and assessing intermediate outputs. We present NeuroImgAgent, a multi-agent platform driven by large language models that translates natural-language requests into workflows for humans, macaques, rats and mice. Quantitative checks and vision-language model assessments determine whether processing continues, enters bounded recovery or stops. Across 268 paired cases, preprocessing metrics were broadly comparable to those of fMRIPrep, AFNI and RABIES. With GPT-5.5, NeuroImgAgent corrected 111 of 120 induced orientation errors and passed all 52 intent-recognition and planning tasks, 8 of 9 recovery tasks and 11 of 14 tool-construction tasks on NeuroAgentBench. In 120 paired challenge cases, the full configuration increased usability from 76.7% to 92.5%, as assessed by blinded experts, and reduced unusable outputs delivered without warning from 18.3% to 4.2% of cases relative to quality-control ablation.

items.title: Pharmacological co-targeting of Hippo and Wnt pathways induces robust Muller glia proliferation and reprogramming in the adult mouse retina
items.abstract: Reprogramming of endogenous Muller glia (MG) into functional neurons represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of irreversible retinal blinding diseases. In adult mammals, however, insufficient MG proliferation constitutes a primary bottleneck that restricts successful MG reprogramming and impairs retinal structural and functional restoration. Here, we demonstrated that simultaneous chemical inhibition of Hippo signaling with TRULI and activation of Wnt signaling with CHIR-99021 elicited robust proliferation of endogenous MG in the adult mouse retinal explants. Following combinatorial drug treatment, MG exhibited gradual induction of the retinal progenitor marker PAX6 and the bipolar/photoreceptor lineage determinant Otx2, without concomitant elevation of the fibrotic marker GFAP, supporting the initiation of MG reprogramming. Mechanistically, our findings revealed that YAP and {beta}-catenin might act cooperatively to induce the expression of MYC, a core transcription factor governing cell cycle progression and somatic cell reprogramming. Elevated MYC accumulation in MG transcriptionally activated Cyclin D1 expression, which, together with the downregulation of the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1, drove efficient MG cell cycle re-entry and proliferation. Collectively, this study establishes a pure chemical combinatorial strategy to trigger robust proliferation and initiate reprogramming of adult mammalian MG. Our findings provide a feasible alternative approach to promote retinal regeneration and lay a foundation for the future clinical treatment of degenerative retinal diseases.

items.title: Sensory Change Detection Unfolds Within a Shared Low-Dimensional Brain-State Landscape
items.abstract: Detecting behaviorally relevant sensory changes requires the coordination of modality-specific sensory processing with shared attentional and control systems, yet how these processes are organized and evolve across large-scale brain networks remains unclear. Here, we investigated the connectivity architecture and temporal dynamics of auditory and visual target detection using fMRI acquired during matched oddball tasks. Cross-modal partial least-squares analysis revealed a low dimensional architecture comprising two dominant, modality-general dimensions and additional modality-biased components. The shared dimensions distinguished a sensory attention action configuration from a higher order associative and contextual configuration, whereas modality biased dimensions showed distinct organization involving frontoparietal and attentional networks. Projecting these connectivity patterns onto time-resolved BOLD activity revealed a common dominant latent space with graded regions of preferential occupancy across modalities. Overlap-adjusted event-related analyses further showed that auditory and visual targets were associated with a similar initial displacement along the first temporal latent dimension, followed by modality-dependent trajectories, particularly along the second dimension. This later divergence reflected different balances of regional contributions within a largely shared cortical architecture. By integrating dimensionality reduction of high dimensional functional connectivity with network and temporal analyses, our findings link the spatial organization of distributed cortical systems to their evolving responses, revealing how shared brain networks can support both common and modality-dependent aspects of sensory target detection.

items.title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Experimental Psychology, University College London
items.abstract: How does the brain orchestrate its central currency, information, for complex adaptive cognition in the real world? Here we provide a comprehensive investigation into the spatiotemporal structure of qualitatively distinct modes of information dynamics in the human brain under ecological conditions. Applying a novel framework for information decomposition to fMRI data from individuals watching full-length feature films, we reveal a multidimensional large-scale information architecture, wherein different schemes for storing, transferring, and transforming representations occupy disjoint topographic and network profiles. Further, this architecture reveals a computational division of labour, with certain regions acting as generalists that support multiple information-processing schemes and others specialising in a few. We show how these interactions reconfigure over time, coalescing into a structured cycle synchronised by sensory input, whose elements are tuned to semantic kinematics. Finally, we replicate these findings in an independent, large-scale dataset. Together, we provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding the principles that govern distributed computation in the human brain during everyday life.

items.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals that coordinated exploration predicts successful conversation
items.abstract: Conversations among friends are often more dynamic, enjoyable, and wide-ranging than those between strangers. How do friends do this? We propose that inside jokes, shared experiences, and mutual interests give friends an aligned mental map, allowing them to leap between topics without losing each other. Strangers may begin in separate mental landscapes, limiting opportunities for exploration as they take smaller steps to avoid confusion. To test these possibilities, we tracked the dyadic dynamics of friends (n = 60) and strangers (n = 54) as they engaged in a real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning. We employed Hyper-Hidden-Markov-Modeling to project partner's neural states into a shared latent space and to segment them into discrete events. This allowed us to quantify how similarly each dyad represented each event (representational alignment), and how spread out conversational events were in latent space (representational exploration). We tested how neural alignment predicted exploration, how both neural measures relate to the breadth of topics discussed, and how they predicted the subjective experience of the conversation quality in friends and strangers. We found that the more a dyad aligned neurally, the more they also explored. While both neural alignment and exploration predicted the breadth of conversations, only neural exploration predicted better perceived conversation quality. Friends were more neurally aligned, which was associated with more exploration. Thus, when friends brains represent the world more similarly to each other, they tend to embark on more diverse and far-reaching conversations spanning a broader range of topics, all while staying anchored in common ground.

items.title: AAV-Mediated Astrogliosis Recapitulates Early Neuroinflammatory and Bioenergetic Features of Alzheimer''s Disease in Mice
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation and altered neuron-astrocyte metabolic interactions are increasingly recognized as early features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the underlying metabolic adaptations remain incompletely understood. This study employed deuterium magnetic resonance spectroscopy (DMRS) following administration of deuterium labeled glucose and acetate to investigate neuronal and astroglial substrate utilization and metabolic fluxes, respectively, in adenovirus-induced neuroinflammation and early-stage APPNL-F/NL-F mice. In adenovirus-induced astrogliosis, increased acetate derived [4,4'-2H2]Glx (d2-Glx) production suggested enhanced astrocytic acetate utilization and TCA cycle activity. Conversely, reduced glucose derived d2-Glx despite comparable glucose uptake suggested a diminished neuronal activity due to potentially impaired neuronal oxidative metabolism. However, the glucose-derived lactate labeling remained unchanged, suggesting differential effects on oxidative and non-oxidative pathways of glucose metabolism. Similarly, 3-month-old APPNL-F/NL-F mice exhibited significantly increased [2,2',2''-2H3]acetate (d3-Ace) influx compared with wild-type controls, suggesting early alterations in astrocytic substrate utilization. While glucose uptake remained unchanged, glucose derived Glx and lactate showed modest, non-significant decreases, potentially reflecting early alterations in glucose metabolism. Overall, both models exhibited a metabolic pattern characterized by increased astrocytic acetate utilization with trends towards reduced glucose associated metabolism, with more pronounced changes in adenovirus-induced astrogliosis. These findings highlight the utility of DMRS for investigating dynamic metabolic adaptations during neuroinflammation and early AD pathogenesis. Importantly, the adenovirus-induced astrogliosis model recapitulates key metabolic alterations associated with the neuroinflammatory aspects of AD. As such, it provides a valuable complementary platform for investigating mechanisms driving early metabolic dysfunction and evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring neuron-astrocyte metabolic interactions prior to the onset of substantial neurodegeneration.

items.title: Testing hypothesized neural substrates with lesions
items.abstract: Correlative neuroimaging generates anatomical hypotheses causally testable by lesion studies. Regionally weighted lesion volume-deficit regression - comparing slopes of behavioural dependence on damage inside vs outside a hypothesized neural substrate - and compartmental volume comparisons inheriting the same logic have been widely employed for this task, but without analytical examination or empirical validation of the underlying methodology. Here we show analytically that this approach does not provide a valid test of whether the hypothesized compartment identifies the true substrate. To illustrate the empirical consequences, we conduct semi-synthetic simulations using 4119 ischaemic lesions, modelling behavioural deficits dependent on a global lesion attribute, on widely investigated distributed cortical networks and white matter tracts, or on a right frontal substrate of fluid intelligence previously identified by multivariate methods. We apply regionally weighted regression with each hypothesized compartment as the target over 5000 iterations spanning multiple realistic noise levels. Where the hypothesized target is not the true substrate, we find spuriously significant dependence despite definitionally absent anatomical specificity; adjustment for lesion volume attenuates or exacerbates the observed bias dependent on the chosen target. Conversely, where the target is the true substrate, lesion volume correction universally reduces already poor sensitivity. Our analysis potentially explains common discrepancies across localisation studies, and highlights the necessity of multivariate approaches that explicitly model lesion and substrate anatomy at finely resolved spatial scales.

items.title: Historeceptomics Profiling of Ketamine
items.abstract: Ketamine elicits distinctive neuropsychiatric phenotypes from a complex and as yet elusive mechanism of action. Here, we applied an updated Historeceptomics approach to identify molecular targets and brain tissues that may contribute to its antidepressant, analgesic, and dissociative effects. Historeceptomics generates multidimensional target-tissue fingerprints by integrating drug-target activity with tissue-specific target expression, providing an anatomic profile of drug action. The results suggest that ketamine activity on NMDA receptors in the prefrontal and cingulate cortices and the amygdala may contribute to ketamine improvements in social functioning for MDD. However, this same receptor-tissue activity may invoke hallucinatory effects at higher intensity or with engagement of additional brain regions. The central nervous system (CNS) fingerprint for ketamine was compared with those of other psychoactive drugs, showing overlap with fingerprints from other antidepressant, hallucinogenic, and analgesic drugs. Some ketamine effects may be traced to specific enantiomers or metabolites of ketamine. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ketamine elicits its unique phenotype and demonstrate the utility of using Historeceptomics to understand complex drug action.

items.title: Temporal regularity shapes thalamocortical responses and deviance sensitivity in the anesthetized rat
items.abstract: The brain uses regularities in the sensory environment to anticipate upcoming events, but whether predictions about stimulus identity and timing rely on dissociable neural mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we independently manipulated the temporal structure of acoustic sequences (rhythmic vs. jittered) and stimulus deviance of sequence elements (deviants vs. standards) while recording local field potentials (LFPs) and multiunit activity (AMUA) simultaneously from ventral and dorsal medial geniculate body (MGB) and cortical layers in 9 female anesthetized rats. Temporal structure robustly modulated neural responses throughout the auditory thalamocortical system. LFP responses were stronger for jittered than rhythmic stimulation across all layers of both primary and non-primary auditory cortex, with effects spanning early and later poststimulus intervals. AMUA responses showed a complementary temporal-predictability effect in both dorsal and ventral MGB, with stronger responses to jittered than rhythmic stimuli. In contrast, stimulus deviance effects were strongly dependent on temporal context and recording site. Deviant standard differences were enhanced under jittered stimulation in cortex and in early MGB responses, whereas later MGB responses showed a context dependent reversal. Finally, AMUA based Granger analyses revealed sustained jitter specific directed influences from both dorsal and ventral MGB toward multiple cortical layers during the poststimulus period. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal regularity robustly modulates auditory thalamocortical responses and is associated with changes in directed interactions between thalamus and cortex. Responses to stimulus deviance, in turn, depend on temporal context and recording site. These findings reveal distinct but interacting neural signatures of temporal regularity and stimulus deviance in the auditory thalamocortical system.

items.title: Adaptive behaviors emerge from Hebbian-like plasticity through flexible attractors
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior is commonly framed as an optimization problem, in which organisms learn to maximize reward. Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.

items.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of T cells across murine lymphoid, mucosal, and gland tissues
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Excellence in Molecular Cell Science
items.abstract: T cells play essential roles in immune surveillance, host defense, and tissue homeostasis, with their cellular composition and transcriptional states varying across tissues. In this study, we constructed an integrated single-cell transcriptional atlas of 124,186 T cells from seven organs of healthy mice. We identified shared T cell states with distinct tissue associated distributions and transcriptional features. Further analyses revealed transcriptional changes associated with thymocyte maturation, diverse innate-like and memory-like T cell populations in bone marrow, and distinct regional distributions of CD8-like T cell states in the intestine. The submandibular gland contained diverse naive, helper-associated, and effector-associated T cell states. pySCENIC analysis further revealed tissue associated variation in inferred transcription factor regulon activity within shared T cell populations. Together, these findings provide a single cell reference for understanding T cell heterogeneity across lymphoid and non-lymphoid tissues under physiological conditions.

items.title: B cell tolerance is dysregulated in people with complex regional pain syndrome: A high-dimensional immunophenotyping study
items.corresponding_institution: School of Medical Sciences, Brain and Mind Centre, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia
items.abstract: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a devastating chronic pain disorder that typically arises after distal limb trauma. It has a complex, multi-system pathophysiology that is not well understood, preventing the development of targeted therapies. Observations of self-reactive antibodies in CRPS patients that can elicit pain hypersensitivity in rodents have established an autoimmune contribution to the onset and maintenance of CRPS-like pain, although the mechanisms underlying this remain unclear. To understand the development of pathogenic autoantibody responses in CRPS, this study performed the first high-dimensional characterisation of B cell activity in a cohort of 42 CRPS patients and 42 matched healthy controls. Immunophenotyping of peripheral immune cell populations by mass cytometry identified altered frequencies of class-switched and double-negative memory B cell subsets in CRPS, and increased use of autoimmune-associated IGHV1-69 and IGHV4-34 gene-encoded heavy-chains within the class-switched B cell compartment. Additional proteomic and autoantibody assessments identified differences in serum protein and IgA autoantibody profiles that may lead to altered complement signalling and pro-inflammatory cytokine production in CRPS. Together, these findings represent evidence of dysregulated B cell self-tolerance in CRPS that could facilitate production of pathogenic autoantibodies in people with the condition.

items.title: Filtration attenuates cannabis smoke-induced impacts on primary human airway epithelial cells
items.abstract: Rationale: Combustion of cannabis flower and inhalation into the lungs exposes the airway epithelium to toxic particulates and gases. Whether cigarette-style cellulose-acetate filtration, a standard for tobacco cigarettes, attenuates epithelial injury and how it affects cannabinoid capture remain unclear. Methods: Primary human bronchial epithelial cells from four donors were differentiated at air-liquid interface for 30 days and exposed to three cycles of air or CBD- (12.5%) or THC-dominant (20.2%) cannabis smoke generated with or without a cellulose-acetate filter. Barrier function, epithelial denudation, mediator release and epithelial cell protein markers were assessed. Cannabinoids captured from combustion trials of CBD and THC-dominant cannabis were quantified by LC-MS/MS. Results: Repeated exposure to THC or CBD-dominant cannabis strains decreased barrier function, increased epithelial cell denudation, and resulted in greater cell death. Filtration significantly impeded changes in barrier function, epithelial denudation, and cell-death after exposure to both cannabis products. Filtration reduced THC smoke-induced IL-33, Fas, and TRAIL. Soluble CBD and THC concentrations did not differ significantly between filtered and unfiltered combustion. Despite reducing acute epithelial cell injury and mediator release, filtered smoke did not prevent changes in epithelial cell marker expression profiles. Conclusion: Cellulose-acetate filtration attenuated acute cannabis-smoke-induced epithelial injury and selected mediator responses but did not prevent changes in epithelial cell marker expression profiles associated with differentiated cell states. Measured soluble cannabinoid concentrations did not differ significantly between filtered and unfiltered combustion experiments. Cellulose-acetate filters therefore present a promising harm-reduction strategy for cannabis flower combustion, although it should be noted that like tobacco smoke, negative impacts of cannabis combustion are likely to persist even with filtration.

items.title: IPF Patient Derived Lung Macrophages are Crucial In Signaling Fibroblast Activation and Disease Pathogenesis
items.abstract: The role of lung macrophage-generated paracrine signals such as TGFb in activating fibroblasts in the pathogenesis of Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in humans remains uncertain. Here, employing lung macrophages derived from Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) patients and genomic, proteomic and cell function analysis of macrophages, we showed increased generation of TGFb over a period of 48 hours indicative of aberrantly activated macrophages. In cell culture studies, we demonstrated that macrophages markedly activated lung fibroblasts. By inducing actin reorganization in fibroblasts coupled to increased membrane tension, cell contractility, and expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin (SMA) and fibroblast activation protein (FAP). Genomic analysis further revealed augmented collagen synthesis, extracellular matrix (ECM) crosslinking, and activation of pro-survival pathways. IPF macrophages exhibited a threefold increase in surface expression of the mannose receptor CD206, which we exploited using mannose-decorated nanoparticles to selectively deliver TGFb siRNA. The nanoparticle mediated TGFb siRNA delivery prevented these manifestations of fibroblast activation. Genomic analysis showed that TGFb promoted FOXO-mediated expression of COL1A1 in fibroblasts coupled to decreased expression of Matrix Metalloproteinases MMP2 and MMP11. Together, these findings establish macrophage-derived TGFb as a key driver of fibroblast activation in human IPF and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of macrophage-targeted nanoparticle-mediated gene silencing.

items.title: A dynamic role for the apical extracellular matrix in cell migration during Drosophila abdominal morphogenesis
items.abstract: Cell migration plays a central role in development, ensuring cells reach their correct destinations. Many migratory cell types require interaction with the extracellular matrix (ECM) to generate traction. While the basal ECM (bECM) is well known for its role in cell motility, the apical ECM (aECM) has mostly been shown to provide structural and mechanical support during morphogenesis and remains less understood. In Drosophila, the aECM is primarily composed of the giant protein Dumpy (Dpy), which interacts with the Zona Pellucida (ZP) domain protein Piopio (Pio). In this study, we elucidate the role of the aECM in the formation of the adult abdominal epidermis of Drosophila. During this process, the larval epithelial cells (LECs) transition from a stationary to a mobile state, in which they migrate directionally, before apically constricting and undergoing apoptosis. Using in vivo 4D microscopy, we examined the role of the aECM in the dynamic behaviour of the LECs. Initially, a layer of Dpy and Pio is located apically to the stationary LECs. As migration begins, the LECs leave behind this early layer while depositing an additional, morphologically distinct layer of Dpy. Knock-down of Dpy or Pio leads to the detachment of stationary LECs from the early layer and, subsequently, to impaired LEC migration. Our results reveal that the aECM transitions from acting as an anchoring scaffold to supporting cell migration. This functional change is closely linked to the change in LEC behaviour. Together, these findings identify the aECM as a substrate for cell migration and highlight a dynamic role of the aECM during morphogenesis.

items.title: Mitochondria morphology changes dynamically during germ cell differentiation and under chemical stress in C. elegans: a quantitative ultrastructural study.
items.corresponding_institution: INSERM, Centre de Biologie Integrative, CBI, University of Toulouse, CNRS, UPS, Toulouse, France.
items.abstract: Mitochondrial dynamics are essential for cellular health and fertility, yet how mitochondrial ultrastructure adapts during gametogenesis and acute environmental stress remains poorly understood. Here, using high-pressure freezing electron microscopy and automated quantitative morphometry (EMito-Metrix), we mapped mitochondrial ultrastructure across the Caenorhabditis elegans germline and somatic tissues. We reveal that mitochondria undergo progressive structural maturation during germ cell differentiation, transitioning from small, round profiles to elongated networks with aligned cristae. Following short oxidative stress, differentiating germ cells and early embryos, unlike somatic or sperm cells, undergo a remarkable morphological remodeling to form protective, fusion-dependent donut-shaped and vacuolated spheroid mitochondria. Genetic disruption of the mitochondrial fusion factor fzo-1 blocks this pathway and results in a collapse of stress-induced brood size. These results demonstrate that atypical mitochondrial morphotypes are not passive markers of damage, but an active, FZO-1-dependent defense strategy shielding female gametes. This work highlights the C. elegans gonad as a versatile model to explore mitochondrial plasticity, reproductive aging, and environmental toxicology.

items.title: BPEA integrates pleiotropy and epistasis to guide allele pyramiding for multi-trait crop improvement
items.abstract: Dissecting the genetic basis of complex traits and pyramiding favorable alleles are central to crop breeding. However, jointly evaluating pleiotropy and epistasis to identify allele combinations that meet multiple breeding objectives remains challenging. Here, we present BPEA (Bayesian Pleiotropy and Epistasis Analysis), a Bayesian framework integrating LD-guided QTL interval identification, joint genetic inference and allele-combination assessment. BPEA uses the joint posterior to estimate the posterior probability of simultaneous improvement (PPSI) between allele combinations and ranks them by mean PPSI. In simulations, BPEA improved interval identification and epistatic interaction attribution relative to comparator methods and maintained high precision in shared-signal detection. When epistasis was present, it reduced mean combination-selection regret by 68.4-86.3% relative to a model without interaction terms. Applications to three rapeseed populations identified shared genetic signals and candidate epistatic interactions associated with seed-quality traits. BPEA also prioritized allele combinations for simultaneous reductions in erucic acid and glucosinolate contents and identified complementary parents for cross design. BPEA thus provides a framework for genetic dissection and genomics-guided crop improvement.

items.title: AMBER: mapping accessible chromatin associations through barcode seed expansion
items.abstract: Accessible chromatin establishes higher-order regulatory structures spanning multiple spatial scales. We developed AMBER, a hydrogel-assisted approach for confined expansion of barcode seeds and subsequent recording of accessible chromatin associations. In mouse brain cells, we characterized the multi-scale regulatory organizations that accessibility alone cannot explain. We identified a subset of genomic regions enriched for inter-chromosomal interactions that also encode proteins engaged in interaction networks. These regulatory hubs are essential for neural function and help predict disease-risk loci and regulators.

items.title: Apples-to-apples transcriptomics: a parent-of-origin-resolved 'Granny Smith' genome reveals how reference choice shapes biological interpretation
items.abstract: The accuracy and reliability of RNA-seqbased transcriptome profiling inherently depends on how well the reference genome represents the genotype being studied, particularly in highly heterozygous, clonally propagated crops with many genetically distinct cultivars, such as apple. Here, we present a chromosome-scale, parent-of-origin-resolved genome assembly and highly complete annotation for Granny Smith (assembly BUSCO = 98.6% both haplotypes; annotation BUSCO = 98.7-98.9%). To test how reference genome choice influences transcriptomic interpretation, we mapped RNA-seq data from sun- and shade-exposed Granny Smith peel independently to three different apple genome references: GDDH13 (earlier-generation), WA 38 (modern-generation), and both Granny Smith haplotypes (modern and cultivar matched). Despite small difference in unique mapping rate, transcriptome analysis using the modern references showed greater agreement in differentially expressed gene families than GDDH13, while the cultivar-matched Granny Smith references recovered additional functional responses associated with oxidative stress, cuticle biology, and other processes relevant to sun exposure and cold storage. Importantly, many responses were consistent with previously identified metabolomic patterns from the same experimental material, providing independent biological support for signals recovered with the matched reference. Reference-dependent differences were greatest for the subtle sun-exposure storage interaction, indicating reference limitations become more consequential as biological contrasts become finer. Orthogroup-based analyses further showed that both reference-generation differences and paralog representation contribute to cross-genome disagreement. Together, these results demonstrate that seemingly modest differences in mapping performance can substantially alter biological conclusions and highlight the value of high-quality, genotype-matched references for resolving cultivar-specific stress and postharvest physiology in heterozygous perennial crops.

items.title: Causal regulators of human T-cell and macrophage activation from perturbation screens, and a replicated coupling of T-cell exhaustion markers with macrophage M1 activation in patients under checkpoint blockade
items.abstract: Engineering anti-tumour immunity requires knowing which genes control T-cell and macrophage programs, and how the two compartments relate to each other in patients. We built ImmunoTwin, an analysis framework that addresses both questions with public data and with every test, baseline and criterion fixed before the result was computed. From a genome-scale CRISPR-interference Perturb-seq in primary human CD4+ T cells (22 million cells, four donors) we derive a map of regulators of the cytotoxic effector program that is calibrated, reverses direction under CRISPR activation (rho = -0.53), and tracks interferon-gamma production among the hits of independent sorting-based screens (rho = 0.69). From a Perturb-seq in primary human macrophages we recover the TLR4-NF-kappaB pathway as regulator of the lipopolysaccharide response (pathway-level P = 0.0004) and find that transcriptional effects track TNF protein measured in independent donors (rho = 0.58). In both cell types, however, a generic measure of perturbation strength recovers the hits of functional screens better than the program-specific effect (area under the ROC curve 0.96 versus 0.73 in T cells; 0.87 versus 0.72 in macrophages). In 90 patients from seven cohorts with tumour sampled before and during checkpoint blockade, T-cell and macrophage programs shifted together, most strongly T-cell exhaustion markers and the macrophage M1 program (r = 0.43). Fixed as a hypothesis and tested once in 86 further patients from six cohorts, this association replicated (r = 0.51, permutation P = 0.0001) and was specific against expression-matched random gene sets (P = 0.004). The baseline state of one compartment did not improve the forecast of the other, so the criterion we had set for calling the framework a patient-level digital twin was not met. ImmunoTwin provides two validated perturbation maps, a replicated cross-compartment association in patients, and a caution on how such maps are benchmarked.

items.title: MitoArc: A Reproducible Short-Read Workflow for Human Mitochondrial Genome Analysis with Circular-Coordinate and NUMT-Aware Evaluation
items.abstract: Human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis from short-read sequencing is complicated by nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), circular-reference coordinates, sequencing depth, and variant-caller configuration. We developed MitoArc, a Nextflow workflow that accepts paired-end FASTQ files or pre-aligned BAM and CRAM files, retains available nuclear mapping context, and performs standard and shifted-coordinate processing. It runs Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) Mutect2 and mutserve2 independently and reports mitochondrial quality metrics, NUMT evidence, haplogroups, contamination estimates, functional annotations, consensus sequences, and reproducibility outputs. We evaluated MitoArc using 18 controlled datasets, spanning three technical replicates and six sequencing depths (100x-5000x), with 648 allele-level truth observations. Requiring confident primary mitochondrial mapping eliminated 33 observable synthetic NUMT-associated false-positive calls but reduced recall from 0.894 to 0.796. In a matched evaluation comprising 108 truth observations, standard-only and standard-plus-shifted GATK processing produced identical variant recovery and allele-fraction estimates. GATK recall increased from 0.741 at 100x to 0.917 at 5000x, while temporary working storage increased approximately 20-fold. Against the complete truth set, GATK recovered 548 observations and mutserve2 recovered 311 under the evaluated configurations; mutserve2 insertion and deletion modes were not enabled. The benchmark used synthetic data without a background sequencing-error model. A reduced HG002 dataset demonstrated end-to-end operation of the pre-aligned workflow, subject to incomplete nuclear context. MitoArc preserves caller-specific evidence and the analytical context needed to interpret mitochondrial variants. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/sarvezh1/mitoarc.

items.title: AIO Part I: Interpretable ADMET Prediction for Cyclic Peptides and Macrocycles
items.abstract: Macrocycles and cyclic peptides are increasingly important in beyond-rule-of-five (bRo5) drug discovery, yet their absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties remain difficult to predict owing to sparse data, complex topology, and environment-dependent conformations. Here, we present AIO (All-in-One), an interpretable multimodal ADMET framework combining topology-preserving molecular segmentation with solvent-aware contrastive pretraining. Across repeated cross-validation, AIO performed strongly across permeability, solubility, unbound fraction, clearance, half-life, bioavailability, and toxicity endpoints, achieving Pearson R = 0.87 for PAMPA permeability and AUROC = 0.91 for bioavailability. Case studies of recently approved macrocyclic and cyclic-peptide drugs showed agreement between predictions and reported pharmacokinetic profiles, while segment-level attribution highlighted molecular regions associated with predicted ADMET bottlenecks. Despite pretraining exclusively on macrocycles, AIO also transferred competitively to the small-molecule PharmaBench dataset. These results establish a promising foundation for interpretable ADMET prediction across diverse molecular modalities in drug discovery.

items.title: PDAC BioPortal: An Integrated Web Resource for Multi-Scale Analysis of Pancreatic Cancer Transcriptomics
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits extensive molecular heterogeneity and undergoes substantial transcriptional remodeling across disease and treatment contexts. However, publicly available PDAC transcriptomic resources remain fragmented across experimental modalities, limiting the integrated investigation of molecular programs across biological scales and cellular compartments. Here, we developed PDAC BioPortal, an integrated web-based analytical resource for multimodal interrogation of PDAC transcriptomics. The platform incorporates bulk RNA sequencing, treatment-associated transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. It integrates 349 TCGA-GTEx samples, including a primary tumor-versus-normal comparison of 178 PDAC tumors and 167 normal pancreas specimens; a clinically annotated treatment-associated cohort of 55 specimens (GSE225767); a single-nucleus atlas comprising 224,988 nuclei from 43 patients (GSE202051); and spatial transcriptomic profiles encompassing 23,436 tissue spots from five patients (GSE274103). The platform provides interactive differential expression analysis, over-representation analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, patient-aware pseudobulk comparisons, cell-type-resolved interrogation, and spatial gene-expression visualization. It additionally incorporates PDACopilot, an evidence-grounded natural-language interface connecting user queries with structured datasets and precomputed analytical results. Application of the platform revealed distinct transcriptional architectures across disease and treatment contexts. Primary PDAC exhibited prominent proliferation-associated, inflammatory, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related programs, whereas specimens obtained following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) showed prominent mesenchymal, collagen, and extracellular matrix-associated signatures. Comparison of independent bulk and single-nucleus treatment-associated datasets demonstrated significant pathway rank-order concordance, despite limited linear correlation. Focused interrogation of the NRF2-associated redox network revealed broad transcriptional elevation in primary PDAC, involving antioxidant-response, glutathione metabolism, and NADPH-generating genes. Treatment-associated bulk transcriptomes exhibited selective remodeling of individual network components rather than uniform expression changes. At single-nucleus resolution, NFE2L2 expression exhibited cell-type-dependent patterns, with significant patient-level increases in selected vascular, immune, and endocrine populations across the neoadjuvant-treated cohort and reduced expression in malignant epithelial cells in the standard chemoradiotherapy subgroup. Spatial profiling further revealed interpatient variation in NFE2L2 transcript distribution across treatment-naive PDAC tissues, with differences in the proportion of positive spots despite comparatively consistent expression intensity among positive spots. Higher expression of a selected six-gene NRF2-associated signature was also associated with shorter overall survival, providing an exploratory link between redox-associated transcriptional patterns and clinical outcome. Together, PDAC BioPortal provides an integrated analytical infrastructure for investigating PDAC transcriptional programs across complementary cohorts and biological resolutions. By combining interactive bioinformatics capabilities with evidence-grounded AI-assisted exploration, the platform facilitates cross-dataset molecular interpretation and hypothesis generation while distinguishing transcriptional associations from mechanistic evidence.

items.title: Radiation survival selects clonally restricted NSCLC survivors with impaired metastatic capacity and distinct bioenergetic states
items.corresponding_institution: West German Cancer Center, Department of Medical Oncology, Cell Plasticity and Metastasis, University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany; German Cancer Consortium (DKTK
items.abstract: Radiation resistance and recurrence remain major challenges in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Whether radiation survival enriches for more aggressive, metastasis-competent cells remains unresolved. Using longitudinal cellular barcoding, functional assays, and multi-omics profiling in diverse NSCLC models, we show that fractionated irradiation imposes a strong clonal bottleneck, but recovery follows either stochastic or deterministic trajectories. Despite this diversity, all radiation-surviving populations exhibit increased radiosensitivity and profoundly impaired metastatic capacity, including near-complete failure in lung colonization in vivo. Transcriptomic and metabolic analyses reveal three distinct bioenergetic states, hypermetabolic, energy-conserving, and metabolically suppressed, each supported by unique transcriptional programs. Crucially, clonal dominance does not predict molecular or functional state, indicating that clonal selection and post-irradiation reprogramming are decoupled. These findings challenge the assumption that radiation selects for aggressive clones and reveal that radiation survival may instead create a state of post-irradiation vulnerability. This has important implications for therapy: targeting adaptive pathways, not just resistant clones, may improve outcomes.

items.title: Connexin43 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and organelle stress in BRAF-mutant melanoma cells
