items.corresponding_institution: CellCOM Research Group, Center for Research in Nanomaterials and Biomedicine (CINBIO), University of Vigo, Vigo, Spain
items.abstract: Metabolic flexibility helps cancer cells survive targeted therapy, and BRAF-mutant melanoma rewires mitochondrial metabolism in response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKi). We previously showed that connexin43 (Cx43) acts as a tumour suppressor in BRAF-mutant melanoma and enhances the response to BRAF/MEKi. Here, we investigated whether mitochondrial remodelling contributes to these effects. Cx43 upregulation promoted mitochondrial biogenesis including selective increase of CI and CV, enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, alongside DRP1-associated mitochondrial fragmentation. Despite enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS, Cx43 upregulation was associated with respiratory chain remodelling, characterised by loss of complex IV, increased ER and mitochondrial stress, and enhanced mTORC1-associated signalling. These changes were accompanied by an adaptive unfolded protein response that did not engage the pro-apoptotic ATF4-CHOP axis. Notably, BRAF/MEK inhibition largely attenuated the mitochondrial biogenesis phenotype and most of the stress markers associated with Cx43 upregulation, while promoting mitochondrial network elongation and markedly increasing mitochondrial ROS. Despite this impact, Cx43-expressing tumour cells retained higher membrane potential, ROS levels and survival under glucose-limiting conditions. Collectively, these findings reveal a dissociation between the mitochondrial effects of Cx43 and its enhancement of the response to BRAF/MEKi, highlighting the complexity of Cx43-mediated metabolic regulation in BRAF-mutant melanoma. By distinguishing mitochondrial remodelling from therapeutic sensitisation, this study provides new insights into the response to BRAF/MEK inhibition and highlights mTORC1-associated signalling and mitochondrial oxidative stress as potential therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

items.title: Surrogate Verifiers Shape Decisions in Closed-Loop Experimental Design
items.abstract: High throughput, automated screening has revolutionized biological experimentation and prompted predictions of AI-enabled "self-driving" labs. Deployed autonomous lab systems typically use a learned surrogate to predict new experimental candidates and rank which conditions deserve expensive follow-up. Determining whether a computational surrogate verifier can substitute for an experimental assay's ground truth requires an understanding of model accuracy, uncertainty, and extrapolation. In this work, we present surrogate verifiers trained on N=7,688 Lacticaseibacillus growth curves exploring a 10-dimensional media component experimental design space. We train surrogate models across six distinct families including polynomial, Gaussian-process, tree-ensemble, neural, and Monod-kinetic forms to predict maximum optical density (OD600). Surrogates ranked by the most commonly reported accuracy metrics (held-out R^2; MAE; RMSE) disagree sharply on which experiments to test next and the best achievable yield. We evaluate models in a Bayesian optimization loop and find that the model used as the active learning oracle matters more than the acquisition function or batch size. We apply conformal calibration to build a model-agnostic assessment criterion of uncertainty and model coverage. We end by evaluating model accuracy and calibration under transfer to an unseen related bacterial strain, and confirm on a prospective validation plate that the transferred verifier's intervals fail in the direction and region our retrospective analysis predicts. This work explores the surrogate verifier within the loop as a previously underexplored axis of closed-loop design and points towards best calibration practices.

items.title: Sex-dependent gating of astrocyte-driven nociceptive plasticity
items.corresponding_institution: Medical University of Vienna, Center for Brain Research, Division of Neurophysiology
items.abstract: Sex differences in pain are well established, yet how nociceptive processing is differentially regulated across sexes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that spinal astrocytes provide pathway-specific control of acute nociceptive synaptic plasticity in rats. Chemogenetic activation of distinct astrocytic G-protein-coupled receptor pathways induced synaptic depression or potentiation at spinal nociceptive synapses in males, but failed to evoke detectable plasticity in females. Despite this lack of astrocyte-induced synaptic plasticity, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity comparable to males, revealing a dissociation between synaptic plasticity and pain-related behavior. Gonadectomy prevented astrocyte-induced plasticity in males, whereas testosterone treatment enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in ovariectomized females. Females exhibited more prominent perineuronal net labeling, and enzymatic degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in females. Together, these findings identify hormonal status and ECM organization as important determinants of the susceptibility of spinal nociceptive circuits to astrocyte-driven synaptic plasticity.

items.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
items.abstract: Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

items.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
items.abstract: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

items.title: ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 coordinates lipid homeostasis to support autophagosome formation
items.abstract: Autophagosome formation requires cells to mobilize lipids for phagophore expansion and completion while maintaining lipid homeostasis during nutrient stress. How lipid intermediates are partitioned between membrane synthesis and neutral lipid storage under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 as a regulator of starvation-induced autophagy in budding yeast. Loss of Mdm1 reduced autophagic flux despite preserved TORC1 responses to starvation and impaired autophagosome completion, as indicated by the accumulation of perivacuolar Atg8-positive structures and reduced protease protection. Lipidomic analyses revealed decreased phosphatidylinositol (PI) in whole cells and Atg8-enriched membrane fractions, accompanied by increased diacylglycerol (DAG) and storage lipids. Derepression of phospholipid synthesis through OPI1 deletion or inhibition of triacylglycerol synthesis restored autophagic flux. Remarkably, exogenous DAG also rescued autophagy despite elevated endogenous DAG in Mdm1-deficient cells. DAG supplementation increased PI abundance and improved protease protection, linking changes in lipid metabolism to autophagosome completion. Together, these findings implicate Mdm1 in coordinating membrane phospholipid homeostasis with neutral lipid metabolism and suggest that the metabolic availability of lipid intermediates contributes to efficient autophagosome formation during starvation.

items.title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice
items.abstract: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.

items.title: Cell-type-resolved methylation analysis using bulk long-read sequencing across human tissues
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: DNA methylation shapes cellular identity and changes with aging and disease, but most human methylomes come from bulk tissue, which mixes signal across many cell types. A methylation change at the bulk tissue level can reflect a change in cellular composition or an intrinsic shift within a cell type, and the two cannot be separated from bulk data. Single-cell and sorted-cell methods resolve cell types directly, but their cost and workflow complexity pose challenges to large studies. Long-read sequencing of single DNA molecules can directly detect DNA methylation on each read. We built COMET (Cell-of-Origin from METhylation), a framework that uses cell-type-specific methylation to assign individual long reads to cell types from standard bulk long-read sequencing. COMET detects changes in cell-type composition robustly even from shallow bulk long-read data, quantifies methylation level of repetitive DNA within each cell type, and, with deeper sequencing, resolves methylation differences between health and disease in individual cell types. We applied COMET to 140 human blood samples, 104 human brain samples and 59 human colon samples. In blood, we found epigenetic aging clock is primarily driven by shifts in cell-type composition, and that APOE4 carriers have myeloid-specific methylation changes. In brain, we found sex-biased change in cell-type composition with age, resolved methylation and hydroxymethylation separately within each cell type. In colon, we found a consistent expansion of fibroblasts in tumors relative to matched normal tissue, localized methylation loss at LINE-1 in fibroblast cells, and identified tumor- and cell-type-specific hypermethylation in epithelial cells at the promoters of known colorectal cancer genes. By resolving cell-type-specific methylation directly from bulk long-read data, this approach opens broad study of cell-type epigenetics across human tissues in aging and disease.

items.title: Haplotype reconstruction in multi-generational diploid and tetraploid populations
items.abstract: Previously, we developed a statistical framework and software (PolyOrigin1) to reconstruct parental haplotypes of each offspring in connected tetraploid F1 populations. A key application of the technology is quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping, via regression of phenotypes on posterior probabilities of parental origins. In this work, we extend the methodology and software (PolyOrigin2) to multi-generational populations (both diploid and tetraploid), which are common in breeding programs. The extension links parental origins across generations to estimate posterior probabilities of founder origins. Compared to PolyOrigin1, the main challenge is to phase intermediate individuals that are both parents and offspring, which is overcome by the Bayesian update rule. In addition, genotypic error models are extended to account for sequencing errors such as allelic bias and overdispersion in genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS). Extensive simulations were used to compare PolyOrigin2 with previous methods and to study the effects of such variables as sequencing errors and the number of progeny per parent. We further evaluated PolyOrigin2 using three real datasets: diploid potato with 23 founders and 7 generations, tetraploid potato with 10 founders and 3 generations, and tetraploid blueberry with 10 founders and 4 generations. The results show that PolyOrigin2 is accurate for haplotype phasing and reconstruction in diploid and tetraploid pedigrees and opens new opportunities for haplotype-based QTL mapping.

items.title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
items.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

items.title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
items.corresponding_institution: Istanbul Medipol Universitesi Uluslararasi Tip Fakultesi
items.abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

items.title: Common organization of collective dynamics across divergent self-organized neural architectures
items.abstract: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.

items.title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
items.corresponding_institution: Imaging Genetics Center, Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, Marina del Re
items.abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

items.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
items.corresponding_institution: Douglas Hospital Research Centre, McGill University
items.abstract: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

items.title: Single-cell analysis identifies concurrent type 2 and interferon programs in experimental eosinophilic esophagitis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, type 2 cytokine-driven allergic disease of the esophagus. How the immune and structural cell landscape of the esophagus changes between healthy and inflamed tissue requires further investigation. Methods: CD45-enriched esophageal cells from naive and oxazolone (OXA)-challenged wild-type mice were profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. A cytokine-gated gene expression score identified type 2 program-high cells. Findings were compared with published human esophageal datasets, validated histologically, and examined in Il13ra1-/- mice. Results: A total of 62,245 esophageal cells were analyzed. ILC2s accounted for most type 2 cytokine-expressing lymphocytes in naive mice, whereas Th2 cells accounted for approximately 80% following OXA challenge. ILC2s concurrently lost Il5, Il13 and Gata3 expression while retaining Areg. Resident memory-like CD8 T cells became the largest lymphoid population. Mast cells switched from a connective tissue-type to a mucosal-type and partly cycling state, which was confirmed by increased MCPT1 cells. Esophageal eosinophils displayed a signature resembling skin eosinophils of atopic dermatitis rather than gastrointestinal eosinophils. Il13ra1-/- mice were protected from epithelial proliferation, thickening and eosinophilia. An interferon-associated program characterized lymphoid, myeloid and structural compartments, and its epithelial component was conserved in human EoE. Conclusions: Th2 cells and mucosal-type mast cells are the dominant sources of type 2 cytokines in experimental EoE. This study further identifies a conserved interferon-associated program that accompanies the type 2 response in the immune and structural compartments of the esophagus and highlights it as a candidate contributor to EoE pathology.

items.title: Continuous karyotypic and cryptic structural fluctuations drive acral melanoma evolution
items.abstract: Reliable chromosome segregation during mitosis is essential for high-fidelity mammalian cell division. Even human cancers burdened by whole genome duplication and aneuploidy generally retain sufficiently stable segregation to produce clonal populations of progeny. Cancer genomes are accordingly understood to evolve in punctuated bursts, in which catastrophic rearrangement is followed by clonal expansion of a stabilized karyotype. However, bulk genomic sequencing, the workhorse of cancer genetics for the past two decades, cannot resolve structural variability within tumor subpopulations. Here we identify a subset of cancers that exhibit continuous ultra-low fidelity chromosomal segregation, with single tumors harboring individual cells whose metaphase chromosome counts ranged from 25 to over 200. This remarkable phenotype is recurrent in multiple cancer types and most common in acral melanoma, where it is associated with dicentric chromosomes, translocations, and complex structural variants. Single-cell whole genome sequencing revealed ongoing structural variation and the genomic signature of microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR), a backup DNA repair pathway that triggers chromoanasynthesis. These genomes therefore do not pass through isolated catastrophic events and settle into stable lineages but rather undergo continuous evolution of chromosome number and structure across generations, resulting in extreme intratumoral heterogeneity and a shifting repertoire of gene fusions. We anticipate these findings will serve as a starting point for classifying tumors by ongoing karyotypic and structural fluctuation and for testing whether this state confers selective dependence on backup repair pathways.

items.title: ASTEROID, A Validated Annotated Dataset of Analytical Decisions in Graph Theory Based fMRI
items.corresponding_institution: Carl von Ossietzky University Oldenburg, Germany
items.abstract: Graph theory-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies use complex analytical pipelines, but methodological decisions are often reported in unstructured text, limiting systematic comparison and the design of multiverse analyses. Here, we describe ASTEROID, a structured annotation dataset derived from 156 graph theory-based human fMRI study publications. Its schema contains 125 labels, comprising 61 methodological labels and 64 labels for study characteristics and experimental design. An LLM-assisted workflow generated initial annotations, which underwent automated quality-control checks and expert human review. The dataset captures preprocessing, functional connectivity, and graph-analysis decisions. Within these categories, steps and their sequence, software, algorithms, parameters, and supporting text spans are included where available. This accompanying paper provides prompt specifications, processing scripts, and documentation, and describes an interactive viewer that supports exploration of the annotation schema and the study records. ASTEROID enables comparison of reported analytical choices, the informed design of multiverse-based robustness analysis and supports the development and evaluation of automated methodological information-extraction tools and educational resources for fMRI data analysis.

items.title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
items.abstract: The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

items.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial (NCT03429075). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

items.title: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants
items.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

items.title: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
items.abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individual's genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

items.title: Excess of de novo substitutions in the genomes of individuals with newly acquired germline TP53 mutations
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX, USA
items.abstract: Inherited defects in the tumour suppressor gene TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a highly penetrant predisposition to childhood and adult cancers. About half of affected individuals carry a variant absent from both parents, and these are the patients missed by family-history-based testing criteria. Where and when such variants arise, in which parental gamete or after fertilisation, remains unresolved, as primary family data are scarce. We addressed this using whole-genome and linked-read sequencing of five family quartets, each comprising a proband with a confirmed newly arisen pathogenic TP53 variant, a closely age-matched unaffected sibling, and both parents, drawn from a cohort of 429 families meeting clinical criteria for the syndrome; matching for age controls for the strong dependence of mutation counts on parental age. Every proband carried a distinct heterozygous missense change in the DNA-binding domain of p53, and read-based phasing traced four of five to the paternal chromosome. Genome-wide, probands carried a significant excess of newly arisen single-nucleotide changes relative to their siblings, which persisted after correction for parental age and was detected on the paternal chromosome. No comparable excess was found for insertions, deletions, structural rearrangements or repeat expansions, and the excess mutations matched the two clock-like processes operating in all cells rather than any distinct mechanism. These features are hard to reconcile with an event confined to the parental germ cells, and instead point to TP53 variants that arise shortly after fertilisation and sweep the embryo, carrying neighbouring mutations with them. Consistent with such sweeps occurring throughout life, TP53 mutations in two large public tumour-genome collections were more clonal than other driver mutations, and the most clonal were present in more cells than the tumour itself, as expected when a cancer emerges within a pre-existing mutant patch of normal tissue. We propose that constitutional TP53 variants and these mutant patches form one continuum, distinguished principally by timing: a sweep during the first cleavage divisions produces a variant present throughout the body, whereas the same advantage acting later confines the clone to one tissue. This reframes a subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome as an early developmental rather than strictly germline event, with implications for testing, counselling and surveillance.

items.title: Complementary DNA-contact and domain-destabilizing mechanisms of PAX9 and MSX1 variants in non-syndromic tooth agenesis: an AlphaFold 3, ThermoMPNN, and AlphaGenome study
items.corresponding_institution: Centro Universitário de Belo Horizonte (UniBH), Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil
items.abstract: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domains of PAX9 and MSX1 cause non-syndromic tooth agenesis, yet most substitutions remain variants of uncertain significance. We investigated the structural mechanisms of 39 pathogenic missense variants in the PAX9 paired domain (n = 32) and MSX1 homeodomain (n = 7) alongside 77 non-coding/splice ClinVar variants. We modelled protein-DNA complexes with AlphaFold 3, estimated folding stability changes ({Delta}{Delta}G) with ThermoMPNN, and compared pathogenic variants with gnomAD v4 domain variants. AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics and mutant interfaces were insensitive to point mutations. Instead, pathogenic PAX9 variants acted through two complementary mechanisms relative to recurrent population controls: loss of direct DNA contact ( 0.564) showed 8%-21% specificity across both domains. Mechanism did not predict missing teeth, whereas missense variants were milder than null alleles (p = 0.001). AlphaGenome matched SpliceAI and jointly prioritized seven intronic variants.
